## Chapter Two: The Classroom Incident

Hoshigaoka Academy's Class 2-C was, by any reasonable measure, a normal classroom. It had rows of wooden desks, a chalkboard that smelled faintly of eraser dust, windows that looked out over the baseball field, and a bulletin board covered in pamphlets for the upcoming Autumn Festival. Thirty-two students sat within it, going about their morning business with the blissful unawareness of people who had not yet been ambushed by sentient gelatin.

Mizuki slid through the door at 8:29, breathless, her hair escaping its ponytail in messy strands, and sat down at her desk by the window with the speed of a ninja.

She exhaled. She was safe. She had made it. The homeroom teacher, Sato-sensei, had not yet arrived. Nobody had noticed her.

She had made it.

Then the soft, bubbly voice spoke from directly beneath her desk.

"Hello! It's me again!"

Mizuki did not scream. She was a sensible girl. She simply closed her eyes, took a long, slow breath through her nose, and asked the universe what she had done to deserve this.

When she opened her eyes, Lumi was pressed against the underside of the desk, sitting cross-legged on the floor (if a gelatinous spirit could be said to sit), her glowing eyes peering up at Mizuki with open adoration.

"You told me not to follow you," Lumi said cheerfully, "but you didn't say I couldn't *stay near* you! So I found a place very close to you. Is that okay?"

"No," Mizuki hissed. "It is absolutely not okay."

Across the aisle, Kaede Morimoto's head snapped up from her textbook. Kaede had long, dark hair she wore in a neat braid, round tortoiseshell glasses, and a notebook full of meticulous diagrams for everything from photosynthesis to the emotional arcs of anime protagonists. She was Mizuki's best friend, which meant she was also the only person on Earth who could recognize the specific twitch in Mizuki's left eyebrow that meant *I am about to commit a crime*.

Kaede's eyes went from Mizuki's face to the shimmering, glittering shape pressed beneath her desk.

"Oh," said Kaede. "Oh, *wow*."

"Kaede, don't," Mizuki warned.

"What is that? Is that a *slime*? Is it a slime? Mizuki, why does it have a *ribbon*?"

"I am aware of the ribbon."

Lumi waved one gelatinous hand at Kaede. Glitter fluttered from her fingertips. "Hello! I'm Lumi! I'm Mizuki's new friend! Are you her friend too? You look very smart. Your soul is like a library!"

Kaede blinked behind her glasses. "My soul is like a... thank you? I think?"

"You're welcome!"

At that moment, the door slid open with a crisp *shff*, and a voice cut through the classroom like a blade.

"Good morning, class. Why is there a glowing blob in the room?"

Every head turned. Standing in the doorway, arms folded, was Akane Kujo, class representative, straight-A student, captain of the kendo club, and the most terrifyingly composed girl in the entire second year. Her hair fell in a perfect black curtain down her back. Her uniform was pressed to a razor's edge. She had the cold, dignified poise of a noblewoman from a historical drama, and she was currently looking at Lumi the way a cat looks at a cucumber.

"That," Akane said, "is not permitted on school grounds."

"Hi!" Lumi bounced up from beneath the desk, all sparkles and light, and waved enthusiastically. "I'm Lumi! Nice to meet you! You have a very straight soul. It's like a sword!"

Akane's eye twitched. "I am not impressed by flattery from a... from whatever you are."

"Oh! I wasn't flattering you! I was complimenting you!"

"That is exactly what a flatterer would say."

"Oh," Lumi said, and then, to Mizuki's dismay, her body began to glow brighter, her swirls of gold and teal spiraling faster. "Oh! Akane-san, I think you're *tsundere*! You're very cool on the outside, but inside your heart is very warm!"

The entire classroom went silent.

Akane's face slowly turned the color of a ripe tomato. "I am not—that is *not*—you do not know anything about my—"

"Morning, everyone!" Sato-sensei swept through the door, clipboard in hand, and stopped dead at the sight of the sparkling gel creature bouncing on the floor. He blinked once, twice, adjusted his glasses, and sighed the sigh of a man who had been teaching at Hoshigaoka for twenty-two years and had long ago stopped being surprised by anything.

"Hoshino," he said. "Is that yours?"

Thirty-one pairs of eyes swiveled toward Mizuki.

She stood up very slowly. Her mouth opened. Her mind, usually the picture of organized thought, produced exactly zero useful words.

"No," she said at last. "I've never seen it before in my life."

"I'm Mizuki's friend!" Lumi announced.

"I've never *met* it before in my *life*," Mizuki repeated, through gritted teeth.

Sato-sensei rubbed his temples. "Well. Whatever it is, please keep it under your desk, Hoshino. And if it sheds glitter on my floor again, you're doing janitorial duty until Christmas."

"Again?" Mizuki whispered.

Lumi gave a bright little shimmer of apology. "Sorry, I didn't mean to! It's just that I'm very excited!"

---

## Chapter Three: The Lunch Rush and the Rival's Gambit

By lunchtime, the rumors had metastasized like a bad fungus.

Mizuki had heard at least seven versions of the story already. In one, she had summoned the slime through an ancient ritual performed in the school's abandoned science lab. In another, she was the secret heiress of a shadow organization that bred magical creatures. A third claimed she had been struck by lightning during a thunderstorm and had gained the power to communicate with gelatinous beings. A boy from the third-year class swore on his honor that he had seen the slime eating a whole vending machine.

The real story was far less dramatic. Mizuki had been trying to eat her lunch in peace on the rooftop, with Kaede beside her, when Lumi had sprung out of her bento box.

Not *into* the box. *Out of* it. Mizuki had lifted the lid to discover a glittering, jiggling, delighted slime sitting in her rice, grinning ecstatically and waving a chopstick around like a wand.

"I didn't want to be lonely while you ate!" Lumi had explained, dripping a little onto the tamagoyaki. "So I hid in your lunch! Is that okay?"

"It is absolutely not okay," Mizuki had said, quite calmly, and then had dropped her face into her palms and groaned.

Now they sat on the rooftop, surrounded by fluttering laundry, the wind tugging gently at their hair. Kaede was methodically taking notes in her notebook, a tiny pencil moving with scholarly focus.

"So," Kaede said. "Let's establish some facts."

"Please don't."

"Fact one: you were late this morning because you collided with Lumi at the shrine corner. Fact two: Lumi claims to be a Prismatic Gel-Spirit from something called the Eighth Crystal Realm. Fact three: she can eat food and then produce 'magical bread,' which, for the record, is just regular bread that's been sort of... sparkled."

Lumi, who was sitting on the edge of the roof's railing with her legs dangling over the drop (she did not have legs, but she had a convincing impression of them), looked thrilled to be included. "Yes! Exactly! You're very smart, Kaede-san!"

"Thank you," said Kaede, unable to suppress a small, pleased smile.

"Traitor," Mizuki muttered.

Before Kaede could respond, a shadow fell across the rooftop door, and a voice rang out with the precision of a judge reading a sentence.

"Hoshino Mizuki."

Mizuki groaned. "Oh, come on."

Akane Kujo strode across the roof with the regal grace of a noble heading to a royal banquet. Behind her, two members of the kendo club trailed like loyal bodyguards. She stopped three feet from the picnic blanket, looked down at Mizuki, and folded her arms.

"You have been harboring an unregistered magical entity on school property," Akane declared. "This is a violation of the Hoshigaoka Student Conduct Code, Section Seven, Subsection Three. I am here to inform you that as class representative, I will be filing a formal report."

"You can't file a report on a slime," Mizuki said, looking up with exhausted eyes. "There's no form for that."

"There is a form for everything."

"Akane-san," Lumi said, bouncing happily on the railing, "your soul is so cool and so strong! I bet you're really good at kendo! Do you want to be friends?"

Akane's cheeks flushed a deep crimson. "I do not want to be friends with a slime."

"Oh," said Lumi, and for a moment her glow dimmed slightly, her swirls of color slowing like a sad lava lamp. "I'm sorry. I thought maybe..."

A strange silence fell over the rooftop.

Mizuki, who had been planning to be annoyed for the rest of the day, found herself looking at Akane's face, and something in her chest twisted in an unexpected way. Akane's expression had softened, just for an instant, the way a stern teacher's does when a student apologizes. Then she caught herself and straightened her spine, and it was gone.

"Hmph," Akane said. "I suppose... if you were to stop emitting light at inappropriate times, I might consider not reporting you. Immediately."

Lumi's glow flared back to full brightness so fast that the nearby pigeons scattered in alarm. "Really?! Thank you, Akane-san! You're the best! Your heart is so warm!"

"I did not say I would *be friends* with you!"

"You don't have to! But I'll be your friend anyway!"

Akane turned on her heel with a cry of frustration and stalked off the roof, her two kendo club followers hurrying behind her. The door slammed. The wind whistled through the laundry.

Kaede, who had been watching with an expression of deep scientific fascination, pushed her glasses up her nose. "Mizuki, I think she likes you."

"What? *Akane?* She's always glaring at me."

"Exactly. That's a classic rival-romance setup. She's competitive with you in class. She watches you during kendo practice. And now she's getting a slime to fight over your attention."

"That is not a romance. That's just a slime."

"Mizuki-chan!" Lumi bounced over, sending glitter spiraling through the air. "Do you want to eat more of my magic bread? I made some just for you!"

From deep within her gelatinous body, she produced, with a soft *pfft*, a perfectly golden melon bread, glimmering with tiny sparks.

Mizuki stared at it. It was, undeniably, the most beautiful melon bread she had ever seen.

"...Okay," she said, reaching for it. "Just this once."

## Chapter Four: The Gate, the Crowd, and the Hug

The worst part, Mizuki would later reflect, was not the slime itself. It was the *audience*.

It was 4:30 in the afternoon, the golden hour, when the sun laid long shadows across the school gate and the air smelled of roasted sweet potatoes from the vendor cart by the bus stop. Students poured through the gates in clumps and clusters, laughing and chatting, pulling on backpacks and fixing ties. It was the most crowded moment of the day, and Mizuki, unfortunately, had chosen to walk out at exactly the wrong time.

Lumi had insisted on walking her home.

"It's dangerous out there!" Lumi had said. "There could be monsters! Or bad slimes! Or even... *sad* slimes!"

"There are no monsters," Mizuki had replied.

"There are *so* many monsters!" Lumi had insisted, and then had bounced out of Mizuki's backpack and onto the gravel path, where she immediately began leaving glowing sparkle-trails behind her like a very determined snail.

Now, at the gate, Mizuki tried to walk casually, pretending to be a normal girl with a normal life, while a glittering slime bounced beside her, humming a cheerful tune.

It did not work.

Heads turned. Phones came out. A first-year girl pointed and squealed. A boy from the baseball team dropped his glove. Somewhere in the crowd, a voice whispered, "Is that the slime girl? The one from the shrine?"

Mizuki's face went through several shades of red before settling on a deep, humiliated crimson.

"Ignore them," she muttered. "Just keep walking. Don't make eye contact."

"Mizuki-chan!" Lumi called, spinning in a joyful little circle. "Everyone's looking at us! Isn't it exciting?"

"It is *not* exciting."

"Mizuki-chan, look!" Lumi cried, and before Mizuki could stop her, the gel creature launched herself at Mizuki's chest in an enthusiastic, full-body hug.

It was, Mizuki would later swear, the most mortifying moment of her entire life.

Lumi was warm and soft and oddly buoyant, like being embraced by a very large, very enthusiastic jellyfish filled with fireworks. Glitter exploded outward in a shower of sparks, drifting across the gate and settling on the shoulders of everyone within ten feet. Somewhere in the crowd, someone let out a long, delighted "*Awwwwww*."

"I love you, Mizuki-chan!" Lumi declared into her ear, her voice ringing with pure, unfiltered sincerity. "You're my first friend in this whole world! Thank you for being my friend!"

For one long, excruciating second, Mizuki stood frozen in the middle of Hoshigaoka Academy's front gate, sparkles in her hair, a slime clinging to her like a glowing koala, while two hundred of her classmates stared with open mouths and camera phones raised.

Then, slowly, she lifted one hand, and awkwardly, stiffly, patted the top of Lumi's gelatinous head.

"...Yeah," she mumbled. "You too."

The crowd erupted.

"*AWWWWW!*"

"She's so cute!"

"Is it a *romance*?"

"I knew she had a secret!"

Mizuki groaned into her palms. Lumi giggled and wiggled with joy, sending another wave of sparkles across the gravel.

From the corner of her eye, Mizuki caught sight of a familiar figure standing near the bus stop. Akane Kujo was watching the scene with her arms crossed and her face inscrutable. But Mizuki noticed, with a jolt of surprise, that the corner of Akane's mouth had lifted, just slightly, into the faintest and most reluctant of smiles. When Akane saw Mizuki looking, she immediately scowled and turned away, stalking off toward the train station without a word.

Kaede appeared at Mizuki's elbow, notebook already out. "Okay," she said. "So that's the first official sighting of Mizuki and Lumi as a couple. I'm going to need a full report."

"We are not a couple."

"Mizuki-chan and I are best friends!" Lumi corrected cheerfully. "Forever and ever!"

"Forever and ever," Kaede repeated, scribbling furiously. "This is going to be an *incredible* Autumn Festival."

Mizuki closed her eyes and sighed a sigh so deep it seemed to come from the bottom of her soul.

Somewhere in the Eighth Crystal Realm, she suspected, a very old and very wise council of gelatinous spirits had just made a terrible mistake.

And somewhere inside her own chest, beneath all the embarrassment and exhaustion, a small, warm, traitorous feeling was beginning to glow.

---

## Epilogue: The Festival Begins

Hoshigaoka's Autumn Festival arrived on a brisk Saturday morning, the air crisp with the scent of grilled squid and cinnamon sugar. Paper lanterns swayed between the cherry trees. Food stalls lined the central courtyard. Students in yukata and school uniforms bustled between booths, laughing and shouting and trying to win stuffed animals with flimsy paper nets.

Mizuki stood at the center of it all, dressed as the class's maid café hostess, a frilly apron tied around her waist, a headband with little cat ears perched on her head. She had argued against it. She had lost the argument. Kaede had cheerfully reminded her that losing arguments was simply part of the Mizuki experience.

Beside her, glowing with a happy shimmer, Lumi bounced in place, dressed in a tiny paper crown that Kaede had fashioned from origami.

"Mizuki-chan!" Lumi cried. "Look! There's a yakisoba stall over there! Can we get some? I want to try *everything*!"

"We are on shift," Mizuki said. "We have customers to serve."

"But the festival is so exciting!"

Before Mizuki could argue further, a familiar voice cut through the crowd, cool and clipped and entirely too composed.

"Hoshino. Your table is waiting."

Akane stood at the entrance of the maid café, dressed in a crisp white kimono with a red obi, her hair tied back in an elegant knot. She had, Mizuki noticed, a single red ribbon tied in her hair, matching the one Lumi wore.

Mizuki stared. "When did you—"

"I was asked to inspect the café for safety," Akane said stiffly, not meeting her eyes. "It is entirely unrelated to the fact that I wanted to see the slime."

"Akane-san!" Lumi bounced over and wrapped a glittering tendril around Akane's wrist. "You came! Do you want to be friends now? Please say yes!"

Akane looked down at the tendril, and then at the sparkling, hopeful eyes gazing up at her. For a long moment, she said nothing.

Then, very quietly, she said, "...Fine. But only for today."

"Yay!" Lumi cried, and glitter exploded across the entire courtyard in a dazzling shower of teal and gold.

Mizuki, watching the scene unfold, felt the familiar sinking dread of a protagonist who had lost all control over her life. Her best friend was grinning like a fox. Her rival was blushing like a lantern. And her new, glowing, glittering, wildly enthusiastic best friend-slime was leaping into the air, shouting something about yakisoba and destiny.

She sighed, and then, despite herself, she smiled.

The festival was loud and bright and absolutely chaotic. Her life was a comedy of errors, a parade of mortification, and a cavalcade of unwanted attention.

It was also, she had to admit, the most interesting it had ever been.

"Come on, Lumi," Mizuki said, reaching out to catch the slime's glowing hand. "Let's go get that yakisoba."

"Yes!" Lumi squealed. "And then we can go on the Ferris wheel! And then we can fight a dragon! And then we can save the world!"

"We are not fighting a dragon."

"Maybe next week?"

"No."

"Maybe next *month*?"

Mizuki groaned. But she was still smiling as she led the way through the lantern-lit crowd, a sparkling slime bouncing at her side and her rival trailing close behind, pretending not to care.

And somewhere above the festival, the first stars began to glimmer in the deepening sky, as if the universe itself had decided that this, finally, was the beginning of the adventure.

*Fin.*

# 1.2.2 Radial Direction: Explanation

This section applies Newton's second law along the string of a simple pendulum, the direction pointing from the bob toward the pivot.

## Setup

- A bob of mass $m$ hangs on a string of length $L$.
- $\theta$ is the angle from the vertical.
- Along the string, two forces act:
  - **Tension** $T$, pulling toward the pivot.
  - **The radial component of gravity**, $mg\cos\theta$, pulling away from the pivot.

## Why the right side is $mL\dot\theta^2$

The bob moves on a circle of fixed radius $L$, so it has a **centripetal acceleration** directed toward the pivot:

$$a_r = \frac{v^2}{L} = \frac{(L\dot\theta)^2}{L} = L\dot\theta^2$$

Taking "toward the pivot" as positive, Newton's law gives:

$$T - mg\cos\theta = mL\dot\theta^2 \tag{5}$$

Note that there is no $\ddot\theta$ term here. Because $L$ is constant, the only acceleration along the string is centripetal. The $\ddot\theta$ term appears in the *tangential* equation instead.

## Solving for the tension

$$\boxed{T = mg\cos\theta + mL\dot\theta^2}$$

This is why the text says the equation "determines the tension." It doesn't govern the motion itself. The tangential equation, $\ddot\theta = -\frac{g}{L}\sin\theta$, does that. Once you know $\theta(t)$, Eq. (5) tells you what tension the string must supply.

## Expressing $T$ as a function of angle only

Using energy conservation with release from rest at amplitude $\theta_0$:

$$\tfrac12 mL^2\dot\theta^2 = mgL(\cos\theta - \cos\theta_0) \;\Rightarrow\; mL\dot\theta^2 = 2mg(\cos\theta - \cos\theta_0)$$

Substituting:

$$T = mg\,(3\cos\theta - 2\cos\theta_0)$$

## Physical checks

| Position | Tension | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Bottom ($\theta = 0$) | $T = mg(3 - 2\cos\theta_0)$ | Maximum tension. It exceeds $mg$ because the string must also supply the centripetal force. |
| Turning points ($\theta = \pm\theta_0$) | $T = mg\cos\theta_0$ | Minimum tension. Here $\dot\theta = 0$, so there is no centripetal term. |
| At rest hanging ($\theta_0 = 0$) | $T = mg$ | The static case, as expected. |

For small oscillations, $T \approx mg$ throughout. For large swings, especially with $\theta_0 > 90^\circ$, the formula can give $T < 0$. A string cannot push, so this signals that the string goes slack and the bob leaves the circular path.

# Episode 1: The Girl Who Wanted to Be Wallpaper

My name is Satō Nanami, and my entire life's ambition is to be unremarkable.

I know that sounds sad, but I mean it as a philosophy. Think of the best wallpaper, the kind that is pleasantly beige and holds up the room without anyone ever saying, "Wow, look at that wallpaper." That is me. I am a second-year at Higashi-Midorigaoka High School. I have shoulder-length brown hair that doesn't curl or lie flat and just exists. My grades sit in the comfortable middle of the class rankings, seventeenth out of thirty-four, which I have achieved three terms in a row, and I'm prouder of that than I should be, because it takes *skill* to land that precisely on average. I belong to the Home Economics Club, which has four members and meets twice a month. My favorite food is whatever is in the school cafeteria that day. My hobbies are "listening to music" and "sleeping."

I thought I had it all figured out.

Then, on a Tuesday morning in April, with the cherry blossoms falling like pink confetti at a parade nobody had asked for, I ran to school with a slice of toast in my mouth.

I want to be clear that I am *not* the kind of person who does this. The toast was a last resort, because my alarm had betrayed me and my mother had been yelling "NANAMI, YOUR TOAST!" from the kitchen in a voice that could shatter glass. So I'd grabbed it, jammed it between my teeth, and sprinted out the door with my school bag banging against my hip. I told myself no one would see. It was 8:07 and the morning bell rang at 8:30, so I had time if I didn't stop, and the streets were nearly empty except for the petals swirling in the breeze.

I rounded the corner by the old shrine, the one with the moss-covered stone lanterns and the crooked torii gate, and ran straight into something that was *not* a wall.

It was soft, and it squelched.

"*Pyuu!*"

The toast flew out of my mouth in a graceful arc, did a full somersault, and landed butter-side down, which is the universe's way of telling you a day is going to be bad. I bounced off the thing and landed on my backside on the cobblestones, my skirt riding up in a way I frantically corrected, and looked up.

There was a girl.

I say "girl" the way you might say "sunset" about the northern lights. It was technically correct, but it didn't begin to cover it.

She was translucent. I could see the shrine's lanterns *through* her stomach, bent and magnified like I was looking through a glass of water. Her skin, if you could call it that, was a gel the color of a soap bubble, shifting from pink to lavender to a pale aquamarine and back again, with little veins of golden light pulsing inside her like slow lightning. Her hair was a cascade of dripping crystal, thick ropes of jelly that hung to her knees and *glittered*, throwing tiny rainbow shards across the stones. Her eyes were enormous, easily twice the size they should have been, and inside them floated actual stars, little four-pointed sparkles that rotated lazily. She wore what appeared to be a dress made of frozen dewdrops, and when she moved, she dripped *glitter* instead of water.

She also had my toast. It had been absorbed into her chest, where it floated in the gel, rotating slowly like a specimen in a jar.

"Ooooooh," the girl breathed, and a small spark jumped from her fingertip to the stone lantern, which hummed. "*You* fell from the sky!"

"I... what? No. I ran into *you*. That's not... I mean, I'm sorry, I didn't see..."

She grabbed both my hands. They were cool and wet and incredibly squishy, like holding two water balloons filled with pudding, and my whole arm went numb with static.

"You are the one!" she cried. "The one from the *prophecy!* I felt your heart-glow from three villages away!"

"There are no villages," I said weakly. "This is a suburb."

"Pururun!" she announced, pointing at herself with a flourish that sent a spray of sparkles into my face. "That's my name! Pururun of the Prismatic Deep! And you..." She squinted and the stars in her eyes went cross-eyed with concentration. "...you are my *best friend!*"

"I'm sorry, what."

"Best! Friend! Forever!"

And then she hugged me.

I must explain what it is like to be hugged by a slimegirl, because I think it will help you understand what came next. It is like being wrapped in a warm, sparkling, ticklish blanket that smells faintly of cotton candy and ozone. My uniform became damp and coated in glitter within two seconds. My hair, which had been tragically average, now crackled with static and stood out in a halo. I could feel her heartbeat, a slow, bright *thrum-thrum-thrum* inside the gel, and sparks leapt off her and danced along my sleeves.

I did the only sensible thing a person could do in this situation.

I screamed, "I'M GOING TO BE LATE!" and ran.

Pururun, of course, followed.

---

# Episode 2: Extremely Visible

The thing about trying to be wallpaper is that it requires the *absence* of glitter.

By the time I reached the school gates, I had left a trail. Not a figurative one. A literal, shimmering, impossible-to-ignore trail of sparkles across three blocks of suburban Japan. I had tried the following: hiding behind a vending machine (she thought it was a game), pretending not to know her (she shouted, "NANAMI-CHAN, WAIT FOR ME!" which, frankly, undermined this), and ducking into a convenience store (she followed me in and spent four minutes tenderly befriending the automatic doors, which she believed were a shy cousin).

"Please," I hissed, grabbing her by the shoulders as we reached the school gate, "you can't come in. This is a school. There are rules. There's a student council. There's a *dress code*."

"Oh!" Pururun's face lit up. "I have a dress!"

"You can't wear a dress made of dewdrops to..."

*Pop!* A shimmer of light, and suddenly she was in a school uniform. It was *our* school uniform, the navy blazer and pleated skirt and red ribbon, except it was made of crystallized jelly, refracting the morning sun into small prisms on the pavement. Her hair was in twin tails now, each one a waterfall of glittering goo that swayed with a wet *sloop-sloop* sound.

"Perfect!" she chirped. "Now I'm a student!"

"You are *radiating light*," I whispered.

"Thank you!"

"That wasn't a compliment!"

But the bell was ringing, and I was out of options, and so I walked into school with a gelatinous celestial being clinging to my arm like a koala, and I tried, with every fiber of my being, to look like nothing was happening.

I want you to know that thirty-seven students stopped what they were doing and stared at us.

I counted.

Here is what I remember: Mr. Tanabe, the gym teacher, dropped his clipboard. A first-year boy walked directly into the shoe locker. Two girls from the tennis club froze mid-conversation with their mouths open in matching O's. A third-year in the hall actually said, "*Whoa,*" in a deeply respectful tone, like he was at a temple.

And I wanted to die. I wanted the earth to open up beneath my indoor shoes and swallow me. I would have settled for a minor earthquake.

"Hi!" Pururun waved at the crowd, scattering sparkles. "I'm Nanami-chan's best friend! Pururun!"

"*Please stop saying that,*" I whispered.

---

# Episode 3: Homeroom of Doom

Our homeroom teacher, Kobayashi-sensei, was a thin man in his forties with permanent eye-bags and the energy of a deflated balloon. He had survived three PTA scandals, a lice outbreak, and a student who had once brought a live chicken to the culture festival. Nothing surprised him anymore.

He looked up from his attendance sheet. He looked at the translucent, glowing girl standing next to my desk. He looked back down at his attendance sheet.

"Transfer student?" he asked, in a monotone.

"Yes!" said Pururun.

"No!" I said.

"Name?"

"Pururun of the Prismatic Deep!"

He wrote it down. He actually wrote it down. "Family register?"

"Um... pond?"

"Close enough." He stamped something. "Seat's by the window. Please don't leak on the floor."

"Sensei!" I burst out. "She's not... she's clearly... you can *see through her!*"

Kobayashi-sensei removed his glasses, polished them on his tie, and put them back on. "Satō-san, I have been teaching for twenty-two years. Things are not what they used to be. Sit down."

I sat down. The universe, apparently, had given up on explaining itself.

The class erupted.

"WHAT," said a voice from behind me, and I felt my soul leave my body. "WHAT IS THAT. WHAT. NANAMI. NANAMI-CHAN. WHAT IS *THAT*."

That was Hoshikawa Rin, my best friend since the first year of elementary school, an eternally energetic girl with a ponytail so high it seemed to defy gravity. Rin was the kind of person who treated every day like the opening scene of a sports anime, loud and bright and permanently on the verge of yelling a team slogan. She vaulted over her desk, landed in a crouch, and stared up at Pururun with eyes the size of dinner plates.

"She's so SHINY," Rin whispered reverently. "Nanami. Nanami. She's like a *jewel.* Can I touch her? Is that rude? Can I touch you? Are you a gem? A ghost? A new idol?"

"I'm a slime!" said Pururun cheerfully, and held out her hand.

Rin poked it. It squished. Her whole face lit up.

"IT'S LIKE A STRESS BALL."

"Rin, don't..."

"IT'S *WARM!*"

Within minutes, a crowd had gathered. Students poked, prodded, and marveled. Someone started a group chat. The class clown, Mori, tried to feed her a snack, and she absorbed the whole bag of potato chips and displayed them in her torso like a snow globe of chips. Everyone cheered. A girl in the back started *sobbing* with joy for reasons I couldn't determine.

I put my head on my desk and prayed to whatever god governs ordinary people.

"Nanami-san."

I looked up. Tsubasa Ichijō, the class representative, stood before my desk with her arms crossed. She had long, straight black hair, impeccable posture, and the expression of a person who has never once been late and considers it a moral failing in others. Her glasses flashed with the stern light of justice.

"I demand an explanation," she said. "This is clearly a violation of at least four school regulations. Unregistered attendance, uniform modification, disturbance of class order, and..." Her eye twitched. "...*glitter.* On the *floor.*"

"I know, I know, I'm so..."

"B-but it's not as if I *dislike* her," Tsubasa added quickly, her cheeks going pink. "I'm simply pointing out that she's, um, extremely *irregular.* That's all. It's not like I think her hair is pretty or anything. Baka."

"You called me a baka?"

"I did *not!*"

Pururun leaned over and patted Tsubasa's head. "You're sparkly on the inside too!"

"I AM NOT," said Tsubasa, who was visibly vibrating. "I am a *professional!*"

And then, as if the day could not get worse, the classroom door slid open, and a hush fell.

Kisaragi Haruto stood in the doorway.

If you don't know who Kisaragi-senpai is, you've never attended high school in Japan, or possibly in anime. He was a third-year, the vice president of the student council, and the kind of boy who had a faint wind following him around that made his hair sway dramatically. He was tall and gentle, with a smile that looked like warm tea. I had spent three semesters being very quietly, very hopelessly in love with him from a distance of at least fifteen meters, which I considered the *ideal* range for romance.

"Sorry to interrupt," he said in his soft voice. "I heard there was a new student..."

His eyes landed on Pururun. They widened. Then he smiled, and an *actual sparkle effect* appeared around him, which I assume was a coincidence.

"Welcome to Higashi-Midorigaoka," he said warmly. "I'm Kisaragi. If you need anything, just ask."

"Thank you!" Pururun said. And then she pointed straight at me. "This is my best friend! She loves you!"

The room went completely silent.

I would like to describe what I felt in that moment, but language is insufficient. Imagine your face is a kettle. Imagine the kettle has been left on a stove for six hours. Imagine the kettle is also somehow screaming.

"I... DON'T..." I said. "That's... she's mistaken... it's a... a *translation* issue..."

Kisaragi-senpai blinked. Then, softly, he laughed. "Is that so? Well, that's very kind of you, Satō-san."

He *knew my name.*

I died. I died right there, at my desk, on a Tuesday. Rin later told me I made a sound like a whistling teakettle and slid slowly under my desk.

---

# Episode 4: Glitter Is Forever

If you think the mortification ended there, you are very sweet and I envy your innocence.

Over the next two weeks, I learned that having a slimegirl best friend is like having a golden retriever, a fireworks display, and a small child's birthday party all rolled into one, then adding magic.

She followed me everywhere. She waited outside the bathroom. She sat on the windowsill during math class, humming and lightly sparking, while the teacher pretended not to notice. When I tried to eat lunch alone on the roof, a sacred ritual I had maintained for a year, she appeared through the *drainpipe* and shouted, "NANAMI-CHAN! I FOUND YOU!" so loudly that two pigeons fled.

She also **shared everything.** She absorbed my pencil case, then returned it "enhanced," which meant my pencils now glowed in the dark. She "borrowed" my bento and made it sparkle, which technically made it more delicious but also meant I was eating a lunch that was visibly *glittering*, and everybody watched. She tried to tie my shoes using actual rainbows. She fell asleep on my desk in a puddle of lavender goo and whispered "best friend" in her sleep, and I wanted to be mad, but she was so peaceful I just ended up putting my blazer over her.

And of course, the school adored her.

The Home Economics Club, my four-member refuge, doubled in membership overnight. The new recruits all wanted to "cook with Pururun-san." She stirred a pot of curry with her bare hand and the whole kitchen smelled like heaven. The club president, Mrs. Ogawa, a plump woman in her fifties with a fondness for pastries, wept openly. "A natural," she sobbed. "A *prodigy.*"

The track team asked if she could pace them, since she moved like a bouncing ball down the hallway at forty kilometers an hour. The art club begged her to model. The drama club offered her a lead role. The *astronomy* club asked, with great seriousness, if they could study her eyes.

And Rin, my Rin, my dearest and most loyal friend, became her **self-appointed manager.**

"She needs a schedule!" Rin announced, holding a clipboard. "Mornings: public appearances! Afternoons: training! Evenings: snacks!"

"She is not an idol," I said.

"Not YET," said Rin ominously.

Meanwhile, Tsubasa was reluctantly "monitoring" Pururun for regulation compliance, which in practice meant she sat next to her at lunch, pretending to take notes while Pururun fed her pieces of glittering melon bread. I once caught Tsubasa smiling at her own reflection in a puddle after Pururun had complimented her glasses. When I pointed this out, she threw a notebook at my head.

Even the delinquent got involved.

Gōda Ryūji was the terror of the third floor, a towering second-year with bleached hair, a scar over his eyebrow, and a reputation for having single-handedly defeated an entire rival school's baseball team with a single glare. Everybody avoided him. He had a pompadour you could have served ice cream on. I once saw him stare down a vending machine until it dispensed a free drink.

I found him one afternoon behind the gym, crouched in the weeds, speaking in a hushed voice to a very small, very scruffy kitten. Pururun was beside him. She was gently glowing, and the kitten was *purring* against her palm.

"...it's just, y'know," Gōda was muttering, "nobody ever, like, *gets* me. They see the hair and the scar and they think..."

"You're a very good person!" Pururun said brightly, and a heart-shaped sparkle floated out of her chest and landed on his head.

Gōda stared at her. His eyes began to well. Then, in a cracking voice, he said, "...Aniki."

"I'm a girl," said Pururun.

"Aniki," he repeated, and wiped his eyes with a trembling sleeve.

I backed away slowly, the way you retreat from a sacred and unbelievably embarrassing moment.

---

# Episode 5: The Day I Cracked

It all came to a head at the sports festival.

Every anime has one. The weather was perfect: bright blue sky, fluffy white clouds, and cicadas droning in the distance. Banners flapped in the breeze. Students in white gym uniforms and colored headbands crowded the field, shouting team chants. My team was Red. Rin had written "VICTORY OR DEATH" on her headband in marker. I had written nothing, because I'm not insane.

I was in the three-legged race with Tsubasa, a pairing assigned by lottery and one that neither of us had survived emotionally. She tied the ribbon around our ankles with the precision of a surgeon.

"Listen, Nanami-san," she said grimly. "I do not intend to lose. My family has a reputation to uphold. We will move on the count of *three.* Do you understand?"

"Yes."

"I will say *left* when it's left. You will say *right.*"

"Why would I say..."

"*Trust the system.*"

The gun went off. We moved. We were doing it! We were actually doing it! Our steps matched, and the ribbon pulled tight. For one wild moment, I felt a rush of adrenaline, a thrilling sense that I wasn't just wallpaper, that I could be *in* the picture.

"NANAMI-CHAAAAAAAN!"

A voice like a thunderclap of joy erupted from the sidelines. I looked.

Pururun was standing on top of the *announcer's tent*, wearing a cheerleader outfit made of crystallized sugar, holding two enormous pom-poms of living lightning. Behind her stretched a banner she had somehow woven out of pure rainbow that read, in glowing, three-meter-tall letters:

**GO GO NANAMI-CHAN!! SHE'S MY BEST FRIEND!!! ♡♡♡**

The crowd roared. Someone started a wave. Somewhere, a brass band that the school absolutely did not have began to play.

"BEST FRIEND POWER!" Pururun shrieked, and shot a beam of prismatic light into the sky that exploded into fireworks over the field, in the middle of the day, in the shape of my face.

My *face.* In fireworks. Forty meters tall.

Tsubasa and I tripped. We rolled across the finish line in a heap, last place, tangled in the ribbon, with glitter raining down on us like a divine curse. The entire school was cheering. Parents were crying. A news van, which I swear I had never seen before, appeared at the gate.

I lay on my back, staring at the sky, where the last remnants of my face were dissolving into sparks.

"Nanami-san," Tsubasa gasped beside me, her glasses crooked. "I have never been so humiliated."

"Me neither."

"...It was kind of amazing."

I turned my head. She was smiling, a real, crooked, helpless smile, her cheeks flushed with exertion and her hair a disaster. And I couldn't help it. I started to laugh. A great, wheezing, undignified laugh that came all the way up from my stomach. We lay there on the track, two girls in a tangle of ribbon, laughing like idiots while a slimegirl on a tent chanted our names.

I realized, somewhere in the middle of that laughter, that I hadn't felt like wallpaper in a while.

---

# Episode 6: The Color Thief

Of course, there is always a plot.

It started on the first day of the culture festival, when the colors began to go missing.

First it was just small things: a poster's red ink faded to gray, the green of the school's gingko trees drained into dull ash. Then the paper lanterns lost their hues, then the students' uniforms. Everything within the school gates seemed to be slowly leaking into a flat, monochrome haze, like an old photograph.

"Something's wrong," Pururun said. We were standing on the roof, the same roof she'd invaded weeks ago. Her normally radiant body had dimmed, and her glitter fell like dull dust. For the first time since I'd met her, she wasn't smiling. "It's *him.* The Gray One."

"The... gray one?"

She turned to me, and the stars in her eyes were trembling. "I didn't tell you everything, Nanami-chan. I didn't come here by accident. I came *looking* for you. The Prismatic Deep is dying. Something is eating our colors, and the prophecy said that only a girl with a perfectly *average* heart could stop it."

I stared at her. "An average heart."

"A heart with no strong color of its own," Pururun said softly. "That means it can hold *every* color. It can borrow them from the people who love you, and blend them into light." She took my hands. "That's why I chose you. Not despite your being ordinary. *Because* of it."

Something in my chest cracked. It wasn't pain, exactly. It was the feeling of a door I'd kept locked for years swinging open.

All my life, I'd thought of my ordinariness as a shelter. A place to hide. I hadn't realized someone might see it as a *gift.*

"You could have told me," I said, and my voice shook.

"I was scared you wouldn't want to be my friend if you knew," Pururun admitted, and a single droplet of liquid glitter slid down her cheek and splashed on my shoe. "I wanted you to like me for *me.* Not for the prophecy."

I looked at her, this ridiculous, radiant, mortifying creature who had barged into my life and covered it in sparkles, and I understood something at last.

I had been so busy being embarrassed that I'd forgotten to notice I was happy.

"You *idiot,*" I said, and pulled her into a hug, glitter and all.

---

# Episode 7: The Power of Friendship (Obligatory)

The Gray One appeared at sunset.

He was a tall, thin figure in a long coat the color of dishwater, with a face like a blank sheet of paper. He drifted into the courtyard as the culture festival reached its peak, as stalls selling takoyaki and cotton candy dissolved into gray smears, and as screaming students stumbled around in a world draining of everything vivid.

"Color is *noise,*" he said in a voice like a dial tone. "Joy is *clutter.* I will make the world smooth, quiet, and *beige.*"

I'm sorry, but that was the one thing I could not tolerate.

"Excuse me," I said, stepping forward. "I'm *very* beige. I'm an expert. And you are doing it wrong."

The Gray One turned. Behind me, the whole school had gathered: Rin with a baseball bat she'd found somewhere, Tsubasa clutching a stack of rulebooks like a shield, Gōda cracking his knuckles with a kitten in his jacket pocket, Mrs. Ogawa holding a rolling pin, Kobayashi-sensei sighing in the doorway, and Kisaragi-senpai with his sleeves rolled up.

"Nanami-chan," Pururun whispered beside me. "I need your heart."

"You have it," I said. "You've had it since the toast."

She grinned, a wobbly, tearful, dazzling grin. And she dissolved into light, pouring herself into the ribbon at my collar, and a crystalline wand formed in my hand, humming with warmth.

"Wait," I said. "Is this a transformation sequence?"

"Yes!" said Pururun's voice in my head, delighted.

"Is there going to be *dancing?*"

"A little!"

"In front of *everyone?*"

"*Especially* everyone!"

I felt the first ribbon of light curl around my waist. I closed my eyes.

*Fine,* I thought. *Fine. If I'm going to be mortified, I'm going to be mortified* spectacularly.

The world went white. My uniform unraveled into streamers of rainbow. I spun, I swirled, I summoned a heart-shaped aura with *poses,* oh gods, the poses. A skirt of pure shimmering prism bloomed around my legs. Gloves of dew. A tiara of frozen starlight. A chorus of choir voices swelled out of nowhere, and in the distance a banner I hadn't ordered unfurled that said **MAGICAL GIRL NANAMI: PRISM HEART!**

I opened my eyes, struck a final pose, and said the line.

"I am the light that lives in ordinary days! In the name of friendship, I will *color* you in!"

For the record, I did not choose that line. It just came out. It's possible the wand wrote it.

The Gray One recoiled. "Impossible! You are *average!* You are *nothing!*"

"Yes," I said, and I smiled, for the first time truly unashamed. "And that means I have room for everyone."

I raised the wand. And one by one, my friends' lights flowed into it: Rin's burning orange, bright as a summer festival; Tsubasa's cool, steady blue; Gōda's gruff, loyal crimson; Mrs. Ogawa's warm yellow, golden as custard; Kisaragi-senpai's soft green like new leaves. Even Kobayashi-sensei, who sighed and held out one tired hand, offered a faint but unmistakable violet. The colors swirled into the wand, a rainbow engine, until my whole body blazed.

"PRISM HEART..." I cried, and the whole school joined me in a chorus that I will carry to my grave:

"**...FRIENDSHIP FLASH!!!**"

The light exploded. It poured out in a tidal wave of color. Gray crumbled. The Gray One shrieked as the hues washed over him, and underneath the blankness there was a small, lonely, forgotten shade, a little blue, the color of a child's drawing left out in the rain. The light touched it gently, and the figure dissolved with a soft sigh, as though he'd finally been allowed to rest.

Color rushed back into the world. The ginkgo leaves blazed gold. The paper lanterns glowed red. The sky burned orange and pink above us as the sun slid down the horizon.

And then I fell over, because transformations are exhausting.

# Episode 8: Fireworks (There Are Always Fireworks)

That night, the culture festival ended with real fireworks. Of course it did. The whole school gathered on the rooftop, wearing yukata that had somehow materialized, and the sky bloomed with chrysanthemums of light.

I sat on the railing with a stick of candied apple, my hair a mess, my feet aching, and Pururun's head resting on my shoulder, sleepily glowing a soft pink.

"Nanami-chan?"

"Hm?"

"Are you still embarrassed?"

I thought about it. I thought about the toast and the school-wide stare, about fireworks shaped like my face, about the poses, the line, the music. I thought about Rin crying into Gōda's sleeve, and Tsubasa pretending she wasn't holding Pururun's hand. I thought about Kisaragi-senpai, who had turned to me after the battle and said, "That was incredible, Satō-san," in that warm voice, and about how my heart had given a small, polite flutter, and then... settled. Just settled. As if it had realized something better was sitting right beside it.

"Yes," I said honestly. "I'm still embarrassed. I think I'm going to be embarrassed for the rest of my life."

"Oh." Her glow dimmed.

"But," I added, "it turns out I don't mind."

She lifted her head. The stars in her eyes were spinning.

"Wallpaper is nice," I said slowly, trying to find the words. "But I think I'd rather be... a window. Something the light can get through." I swallowed, and my face went hot. "That sounded a lot cooler in my head."

Pururun burst into tears of glitter and tackled me in a hug so enormous that we both toppled off the railing and into the arms of a waiting Gōda, who caught us both while crying, and Rin screamed "GROUP HUG!" and the whole class piled on in a heap of yukata and laughter and sparkling goo.

Above us, the last firework of the night burst into a shape I recognized: a small, round, grinning slime, with a girl in a ribbon beside her.

Somebody had clearly arranged that. I suspected Rin.

I didn't even mind.

# Epilogue: Next Season's Teaser

It's been three weeks, and I'd like to report that my life has returned to normal.

That is a lie. I wake up each morning to find Pururun sleeping in my bathtub, a glowing opalescent puddle humming softly to the rubber duck. My mother, who accepted the situation with the same eerie calm as Kobayashi-sensei, now sets a third place at the breakfast table. The neighbor kids think I'm a celebrity. Tsubasa has started leaving "regulation compliance reports" on my desk that are, upon close reading, thinly veiled fan letters. There's a Pururun fan club with its own newsletter. "It's not me!" she said, popping out of my school bag, where she'd apparently been hiding. She pointed.

On the corner, by the old shrine, stood a small boy made of living flame, blinking up at me with huge amber eyes. Beside him, a girl made of mist and moonlight was curled up in a ginkgo tree, yawning. Behind them, a tall figure in armor made of leaves.

"They said you were the one," whispered the flame-boy. "The Girl Who Makes Friends."

I closed my eyes. I breathed in. I let it out.

Then I looked at Pururun, who was beaming at me with her whole sparkling, ridiculous, perfect face, and I smiled.

"I'm Satō Nanami," I said to the small crowd of magical beings gathering around me. "I'm a completely ordinary high school student. And please..." I took a deep breath, bracing myself.

"...*please* don't make a scene."

Behind me, the sky erupted into fireworks.

Of course it did.

# Long Hair Costs an Olympic Marathoner About 8 Seconds

**Answer: about 5–10 seconds from aerodynamic drag, with a central estimate of about 8 seconds.** This is a back-of-envelope physics estimate. The calculation below uses an elite female marathoner, since long hair is most common in that field.

## 1. Inputs

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Finish time | 2:18:00 = 8,280 s |
| Speed, *v* | 42,195 m / 8,280 s ≈ **5.1 m/s** |
| Body mass | 50 kg |
| Air density, ρ | 1.2 kg/m³ |
| Runner's drag area (C_d·A) | ≈ 0.24 m² (from wind-tunnel and treadmill studies) |

## 2. Extra drag from flowing hair

Hair streaming behind the head behaves like a fluttering flag that is partly sheltered in the head's wake.

- Streaming hair planform is about 0.25 m × 0.15 m ≈ 0.04 m².
- Flapping flags have C_d ≈ 0.1 based on planform area.
- So the added C_d·A is **≈ 0.004–0.005 m²**, with a plausible range of 0.002–0.01.

The extra drag force is:

$$\Delta F = \tfrac12 \rho v^2 \,\Delta(C_dA) = 0.5 \times 1.2 \times 5.1^2 \times 0.005 \approx 0.08\ \text{N}$$

That is about 8 grams-force. It is roughly a 2% increase on the runner's total air drag of about 3.7 N.

## 3. Convert to metabolic cost

- The extra mechanical power is ΔP = ΔF·v ≈ 0.08 × 5.1 ≈ **0.4 W**.
- Muscle efficiency against a horizontal resisting force is about 40%. So the metabolic cost is ≈ **1.0 W**.
- Running costs about 1 kcal/kg/km. That gives total metabolic power ≈ 4.18 kJ × 50 × 5.1 m/s ≈ **1,070 W**.
- The extra cost is 1.0 / 1,070 ≈ **0.09%**.

## 4. Convert to time

At fixed sustainable power, a 0.09% higher energy cost means roughly a 0.09% slower time:

$$8{,}280\ \text{s} \times 0.0009 \approx \mathbf{8\ seconds}$$

| Scenario | Δ(C_d·A) | Time lost |
|---|---|---|
| Tied ponytail, tidy | 0.002 m² | ~3 s |
| Loose hair, central estimate | 0.005 m² | **~8 s** |
| Big, loose, voluminous hair | 0.01 m² | ~16 s |

## Caveats

- **Drafting in a pack** cuts air drag by about 30–50%, so the real loss over a race is probably **4–6 s**.
- **Hair mass may matter more than drag.** Long hair can weigh 100–200 g more than short hair, and more when soaked with sweat. Carried mass costs roughly 1% of time per 1% of body mass. An extra 100 g on a 50 kg runner (0.2%) is about **15 s**, which is larger than the aerodynamic effect.
- **Ponytail swing** costs a little energy and can cause small rotational disturbances, but this is negligible compared with the above.
- **Headwinds** increase the effect with the square of relative airspeed. A 3 m/s headwind roughly multiplies the aerodynamic loss by 2.5.

Decoding a blurry, low-resolution EAN-13 works best as a pipeline: enhance the image, try several decoders on several variants, and accept a result only if its check digit is valid.

## 1. Know the physical limits

- An EAN-13 symbol has 95 modules (bar/space units). The narrowest bar or space is one module.
- Aim for at least about 2 to 3 pixels per module, so the barcode should be roughly 200 to 300 pixels wide. Below that, decoding fails no matter how clever the preprocessing is. Upscaling adds pixels but not information.
- Keep the barcode horizontal or near-horizontal where possible. 1D decoders are much more tolerant of rotation than of blur along the bar direction.

## 2. Preprocessing

Generate several variants, since no single one works for every image:

1. **Crop and localize** the barcode region if you can (see below).
2. **Upscale** 2× to 4× with `INTER_CUBIC` or `INTER_LANCZOS4`.
3. **Grayscale**, then **denoise** lightly (Gaussian blur, or a median filter for salt-and-pepper noise).
4. **Sharpen** with an unsharp mask to counter blur.
5. **Local contrast** with CLAHE to handle uneven lighting.
6. **Binarize** with Otsu's global threshold and with adaptive (local) thresholding.
7. Try **inverted** images, since some scanners expect light bars on dark backgrounds.
8. Try **rotations** of 0°, 90°, 180°, and 270°, and small deskew angles if the barcode is tilted.

## 3. Decoders

- **zxing-cpp** (`pip install zxing-cpp`): robust, with rotation and inversion handling built in. Good first choice.
- **pyzbar** (ZBar): fast and widely used, but more fragile on blur.
- **OpenCV `barcode.BarcodeDetector`** (OpenCV 4.8+): localizes and decodes, and helps with finding the region first.
- **Custom 1D decoder**: sample many scanlines, convert each to run-lengths, and match them against the L/G/R digit patterns. Use the parity pattern of the first digit to recover the full symbol. This is more work, but it lets you use the partial information that generic decoders discard.

## 4. Validate and recover

**Check digit:** Weight the first 12 digits alternately 1, 3, 1, 3, and so on. The check digit is `(10 - sum % 10) % 10`. Reject anything that fails this, since blur often produces plausible-looking wrong digits.

**Single-digit recovery:** If exactly one digit is unreadable, you can recover it from the check digit. Changing one digit changes the sum by w·d, where w is 1 or 3. Both are coprime to 10, so exactly one value of the missing digit satisfies the checksum. Try each candidate and keep the one that validates.

**Multi-pass voting:** If several variants decode to different valid codes, prefer the most frequent result.

## 5. Example code

```python
import cv2
import numpy as np
import zxingcpp  # pip install zxing-cpp

def ean13_valid(s: str) -> bool:
    if len(s) != 13 or not s.isdigit():
        return False
    total = sum(int(c) * (1 if i % 2 == 0 else 3) for i, c in enumerate(s[:12]))
    return (10 - total % 10) % 10 == int(s[12])

def variants(img):
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY) if img.ndim == 3 else img
    for scale in (1, 2, 3, 4):
        up = cv2.resize(gray, None, fx=scale, fy=scale,
                        interpolation=cv2.INTER_CUBIC)
        blur = cv2.GaussianBlur(up, (0, 0), 3)
        sharp = cv2.addWeighted(up, 1.8, blur, -0.8, 0)
        clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=2.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8)).apply(sharp)
        _, otsu = cv2.threshold(clahe, 0, 255,
                                cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)
        adaptive = cv2.adaptiveThreshold(clahe, 255,
                                         cv2.ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C,
                                         cv2.THRESH_BINARY, 31, 10)
        for v in (up, sharp, clahe, otsu, adaptive):
            yield v
            yield 255 - v  # inverted

def decode_ean13(img):
    for v in variants(img):
        for k in range(4):  # 0, 90, 180, 270 degrees
            rotated = np.rot90(v, k)
            for res in zxingcpp.read_barcodes(np.ascontiguousarray(rotated)):
                if res.format == zxingcpp.BarcodeFormat.EAN13 and ean13_valid(res.text):
                    return res.text
    return None

if __name__ == "__main__":
    img = cv2.imread("blurry_barcode.jpg")
    code = decode_ean13(img)
    print(code if code else "No valid EAN-13 found")
```

Check the zxing-cpp documentation for its current options (such as `try_rotate`, `try_invert`, and `try_downscale`). Those can replace some of the manual loops.

## 6. Last resorts

- **Super-resolution** (OpenCV `dnn_superres` with EDSR or ESPCN, or Real-ESRGAN) can help. It can also invent plausible bar edges, so always check the result with the check digit.
- **Multiple frames:** If you have a video or burst, align the frames and average them before decoding. This reduces noise and can recover much more than any single frame.
- **Better capture:** If you control the input, the biggest gains come from a larger barcode in frame, less motion, and more light.

# Robust EAN-13 decoding from blurry, low-res images

Blur turns the problem from "find edges" into "fit a model". The most robust approach is to stop thresholding and instead average, sample sub-pixel, and match against the known EAN-13 structure, using the checksum as a hard constraint.

## Pipeline

1. **Try a strong off-the-shelf decoder first** (`zxing-cpp`, with `try_harder`). Retry on rotations, 2-4× upscales, and sharpened or contrast-stretched variants. This fixes many cases cheaply.
2. **Localize and de-rotate.** Compute Scharr x-gradient minus y-gradient, blur, close morphologically, take the largest contour, then use `minAreaRect` to rotate the bars to vertical. (`cv2.barcode.BarcodeDetector` also works.)
3. **Collapse to a 1D profile.** Average (or take the median of) many rows along the bars. This reduces noise by about √N and costs nothing in horizontal resolution.
4. **Keep grayscale and avoid binarizing.** Thresholding discards sub-pixel information. Normalize with percentiles instead.
5. **Fit the 95-module grid.** Search over start offset and module width, integrating the profile over each module with sub-pixel accuracy.
6. **Soft-decode each digit.** Compare each 7-module window to the L/G/R codebook by distance rather than hard edge widths.
7. **Enforce the checksum with a DP.** Find the minimum-cost digit sequence whose checksum is valid. This corrects errors that blur introduces.
8. **If video or multiple shots exist,** fuse the per-digit cost matrices across frames (sum the costs) before the checksum step.

## Step 1: quick baseline

```python
import cv2, numpy as np, zxingcpp

def try_zxing(gray):
    for scale in (1, 2, 3, 4):
        g = cv2.resize(gray, None, fx=scale, fy=scale, interpolation=cv2.INTER_CUBIC)
        for variant in (g,
                        cv2.createCLAHE(3.0, (8, 8)).apply(g),
                        cv2.filter2D(g, -1, np.array([[0,-1,0],[-1,5,-1],[0,-1,0]]))):
            for angle in (0, 90, 180, 270):
                img = np.ascontiguousarray(np.rot90(variant, angle // 90))
                for r in zxingcpp.read_barcodes(img, formats=zxingcpp.BarcodeFormat.EAN13,
                                                try_rotate=True, try_downscale=True):
                    return r.text
    return None
```

## Steps 5-7: soft decoder with checksum-constrained DP

```python
import numpy as np

L = ["0001101","0011001","0010011","0111101","0100011",
     "0110001","0101111","0111011","0110111","0001011"]
R = ["".join('1' if c == '0' else '0' for c in s) for s in L]
G = [s[::-1] for s in R]
PARITY = ["LLLLLL","LLGLGG","LLGGLG","LLGGGL","LGLLGG",
          "LGGLLG","LGGGLL","LGLGLG","LGLGGL","LGGLGL"]
arr = lambda t: np.array([[int(c) for c in s] for s in t], float)
L, G, R = arr(L), arr(G), arr(R)
START, MID, END = np.array([1,0,1.]), np.array([0,1,0,1,0.]), np.array([1,0,1.])

def sample_modules(profile, x0, w, n=95):
    """Area-integrate profile over each module (sub-pixel). profile: dark=1."""
    c = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(profile)])
    cs = lambda x: np.interp(x, np.arange(len(c)), c)
    e = x0 + w * np.arange(n + 1)
    return (cs(e[1:]) - cs(e[:-1])) / w

def decode_modules(m):
    """Return (cost, 13-digit string) with a valid checksum, min total cost."""
    guard = (np.sum((m[0:3]-START)**2) + np.sum((m[45:50]-MID)**2)
             + np.sum((m[92:95]-END)**2))
    best = (np.inf, None)
    for d0, par in enumerate(PARITY):
        cost = np.zeros((12, 10))
        for k in range(6):
            seg = m[3+7*k : 10+7*k]
            cost[k] = ((seg - (L if par[k] == 'L' else G))**2).sum(1)
            seg = m[50+7*k : 57+7*k]
            cost[6+k] = ((seg - R)**2).sum(1)
        # DP over weighted checksum mod 10; digit index i+1 has weight 3 if odd else 1
        dp = {d0 % 10: (0.0, [d0])}
        for i in range(12):
            wgt = 3 if (i + 1) % 2 else 1
            nxt = {}
            for s, (c0, ds) in dp.items():
                for d in range(10):
                    ns, nc = (s + wgt*d) % 10, c0 + cost[i, d]
                    if ns not in nxt or nc < nxt[ns][0]:
                        nxt[ns] = (nc, ds + [d])
            dp = nxt
        if 0 in dp and dp[0][0] < best[0]:
            best = (dp[0][0], "".join(map(str, dp[0][1])))
    return best[0] + guard, best[1]

def decode_profile(profile):
    p = profile.astype(float)
    lo, hi = np.percentile(p, [2, 98])
    p = 1 - np.clip((p - lo) / (hi - lo + 1e-9), 0, 1)       # dark = 1
    idx = np.where(p > 0.5)[0]
    a, b = idx[0], idx[-1] + 1                                # rough extents
    w0 = (b - a) / 95
    best = (np.inf, None)
    for dx in np.linspace(-2, 2, 21):
        for sw in np.linspace(0.96, 1.04, 17):
            w = w0 * sw
            cost, digits = decode_modules(sample_modules(p, a + dx, w))
            if cost < best[0]:
                best = (cost, digits)
    return best   # (cost, digits); lower cost = more confident
```

Typical use: rotate the barcode crop upright, then call `decode_profile(crop[y0:y1].mean(axis=0))`. For more robustness, run it on several row bands and take the lowest-cost result.

The grid search is slow in pure Python. Vectorize it, or decode with the unconstrained per-digit minimum during the search and run the checksum DP only on the best few fits.

## Further improvements for severe blur

- **Edge-to-like-edge distances.** If you use edge-based decoding instead, measure rising-to-rising and falling-to-falling distances rather than bar widths. Symmetric blur shifts both edges of a bar, so these distances stay accurate while bar widths do not. This is the classic UPC/EAN approach, and ZXing uses it.
- **Deconvolve the 1D profile.** Apply Wiener or Richardson-Lucy with a Gaussian PSF. Estimate sigma by trying a few values and keeping the one with the lowest decode cost.
- **Blur-aware templates.** Render the ideal 95-module pattern, blur it with candidate sigmas, and compare against the profile directly. This handles inter-symbol interference better than per-digit windows.
- **Multi-frame fusion.** For video, align frames and sum the `cost` matrices across frames before the DP. This is far better than voting on final strings.
- **Learned fallback.** If images are truly awful, train a small 1D CNN or CRNN on synthetic EAN-13s (random digits, rendered, blurred, noised, downscaled) and still apply the checksum afterwards. Synthetic data is easy to generate here.

## Practical limits

You need roughly ≥1 px per module (barcode ≥ ~100 px wide) for the soft approach, and ≥1.5-2 px per module for most off-the-shelf decoders. Below that, a digit's pattern becomes ambiguous, and only multi-frame fusion or a known-product lookup will help.

## Prologue: The Most Average Girl in Japan

My name is Sato Mei, and I am painfully, gloriously, *aggressively* average.

I am seventeen. I am a second-year student at Sakuragaoka Private High School, Class 2-B. My grades sit at the exact middle of the class rankings, and I take quiet pride in that. I am a hundred and fifty-eight centimeters tall, which is the national average for my age group. I checked. My hair is brown, shoulder-length, and held back with a single red clip that my grandmother gave me, which is the only remotely interesting thing about my appearance. My blood type is A. My favorite food is omurice. My hobbies include reading shoujo manga under my blanket past midnight, eating omurice, and not standing out.

Especially that last one.

Some girls dream of becoming idols, or winning national kendo tournaments, or being confessed to beneath the legendary cherry tree behind the school. I dreamed of graduating without a single person remembering my name. I dreamed of a nice, quiet office job, a nice, quiet husband, and a nice, quiet cat named Mochi. I had it all planned. I even had a color-coded binder.

So you should understand how deeply, how *cosmically* unfair it was that on the morning of April the eighth, the first day of my second year, the universe looked down at me, at my binder, at my perfectly beige existence, and decided to pour a bucket of rainbow glitter over the whole thing.

Literally.

## Chapter One: Toast, Corners, and the Worst Collision in Human History

I was late.

Of course I was late. I'd stayed up until two in the morning finishing the final volume of *Kiss Me Under the Starlit Greenhouse*, and when I finally lay down I sobbed into my pillow for forty minutes because Rintarou-sama *finally* told Hanako how he felt and it was *perfect*. My alarm clock went off at six-thirty. I turned it off in my sleep. My second alarm clock went off at six-forty. I threw it across the room. My mother came in at seven-fifteen and yanked my blanket off with the merciless efficiency of a woman who has done this every school morning for eleven years.

"MEI! The opening ceremony starts at eight-fifteen!"

I dressed in a blur. Blouse, skirt, navy blazer with the Sakuragaoka crest, red ribbon tied crooked at my collar. I couldn't find my left sock. I found my left sock. It was in the refrigerator. I don't want to talk about it.

I ran downstairs, my bag banging against my hip, and my mother held out a slice of toast with strawberry jam on it, and I took it in my mouth, and I ran out the door, and I swear on my grandmother's hair clip that I did not realize what I was doing until I was halfway down the street.

*Toast in mouth. Late for school. First day of the new term. Cherry blossoms falling.*

I stopped dead on the sidewalk, toast dangling from my teeth, and a cold wave of horror broke over me.

I had read enough manga to know exactly what this was. This was a *setup*. This was the opening panel of every romantic comedy ever drawn. In about thirty seconds I was going to run around a corner and crash into a handsome, aloof transfer student, and he was going to look down at me with cool, beautiful eyes and say something like "Watch where you're going, idiot," and then he was going to show up in my homeroom, and then—

"No," I said aloud, around the toast. "*Absolutely* not."

I took the toast out of my mouth. I held it in my hand like a normal person. I looked both ways down the street. And then, carefully, deliberately, I chose a route to school that had *no blind corners whatsoever*. It was the long way. It went along the river embankment, where the cherry trees grew in a long pink tunnel and the view stretched out wide and open in all directions. Nothing could ambush me there. I was a genius.

The petals were falling like snow. The morning light filtered through them in soft, buttery gold, and the river glittered silver-blue beneath, and somewhere a bush warbler was singing. I ate my toast while jogging, feeling smug.

Which is why I didn't think to look *up*.

There was a sound like a struck bell. Not loud, but clear and sweet and bright, a sound that seemed to go straight through my ribs and ring against my heart. I glanced skyward.

Something was falling out of the cherry tree.

It was the size of a large beach ball, and it was every color at once. It was the pink of the blossoms and the blue of the sky and the gold of the morning and the green of new leaves, and colors I didn't have names for, colors like the inside of a soap bubble, like the oily shimmer on a puddle, like the flash of a hummingbird's throat. It was translucent, and through it I could see the branches warped and refracted, as if I were looking through a prism. Embedded in it, floating inside it, were tiny crystals, hundreds of them, faceted and gleaming like sugar or diamonds or broken stained glass, and between those crystals crackled little threads of light, sparks of electric pink and cyan that jumped and danced and fizzed.

It fell slowly. Gracefully. Wobbling.

It fell directly onto my face.

*SPLORSH.*

I want to describe the sensation accurately, because I've had a lot of time to think about it since. It was cool, but not cold, like the inside of a peach fresh from the fridge. It was soft, like pudding, but it had a springiness to it, a bounce, like the world's most luxurious gummy candy. It smelled faintly of strawberries, ozone, and something I can only describe as *the color lavender*. And it *tingled*. Every place it touched me fizzed pleasantly, like I'd been dipped in soda.

I went down. My bag went flying. My toast went flying. I lay on my back on the cherry-petal-covered embankment path, my face and upper body engulfed in a quivering mass of luminous goo, staring up through a lens of rainbow jelly at the sky.

And the jelly *looked back at me*.

Two eyes opened in it. Right in front of my face. They were enormous and round, like the eyes of a character in a shoujo manga, the kind of eyes that take up a third of the face. They were a deep, glimmering violet, with star-shaped highlights in them. Actual stars. Little five-pointed sparkles drifting around in the irises.

The eyes blinked. Slowly. Wonderingly.

Then, beneath them, a mouth formed. A tiny, curved, delighted mouth.

"*Ah,*" said the slime, in a voice like wind chimes and ramune bottles and a little girl's laughter. "*It's you.*"

I screamed.

I screamed so loudly that a flock of pigeons exploded out of the cherry trees and an old man walking his shiba inu on the far bank dropped the leash. I flailed. I kicked. I tried to push the slime off me, but my hands sank into it up to the wrists, and it wrapped around them warmly, gently, and squeezed, like it was holding my hands.

"Get off! Get OFF! What ARE you?!"

The slime slid off my face and pooled on my chest, then rose up, gathering itself, coalescing, pulling inward and upward with a sound like a jelly dessert being turned out of a mold. I scrambled backward on my elbows and watched, mouth hanging open, as the shapeless blob *became a girl*.

She was about my height. Maybe a little shorter. She had long hair, or something like hair, that fell to her waist in thick, glossy, liquid ropes, each one a different gradient of color: rose to tangerine, mint to sapphire, lemon to lilac. The ends of her hair dripped, but the drips never fell; they just stretched and bounced back up like yo-yos. Her body was shaped like a girl's, slender and soft, and it was still translucent, so I could see the cherry blossoms behind her through her torso, and the crystals were still inside her, drifting like flakes in a snow globe. They clustered more densely around her chest, where a single larger crystal, the size of a plum and shaped like a heart, pulsed with a slow, warm, rose-gold light.

Her heart. That was her *heart*. I could see it *beating*.

She'd formed herself a kind of dress, or the impression of one: a frilly, ruffled shape at her waist like a petticoat made of jelly, in shades of pink and seafoam. Glitter drifted off her constantly, a fine shimmering mist that caught the sunlight and threw it everywhere. When she moved, little sparks jumped from her fingertips and crackled in the air. *Pchk. Pchk-pchk.*

She looked down at me with those enormous starry eyes, clasped her jelly hands beneath her chin, and the heart crystal in her chest flared so bright it lit up my face pink.

"I found you," she breathed. "I fell from the stars and the first thing I saw was *you*. You have to be my best friend now. That's the rule."

"That is *not* the rule!"

"It's the rule," she said serenely, and sparkled at me.

I looked down at myself. My blazer was coated in a layer of fine iridescent glitter. My hair was sticky. My ribbon had turned a gentle shade of periwinkle. My skirt shimmered like the scales of a koi. I looked like I'd been attacked by a fairy's craft bin.

Far away, faint and tinny, I heard the school bell.

"No," I whispered. "Nonononono—"

## Chapter Two: Please Welcome Our New Transfer Student (Who Is a Puddle)

I ran. I didn't know what else to do. I grabbed my bag, abandoned the toast to the pigeons, and sprinted toward Sakuragaoka High as fast as my average legs could carry me, trailing glitter like a comet trails ice.

The slime girl came with me.

She didn't run, exactly. She *bounced*. She'd collapse into a ball and spring along beside me in big, joyous arcs, *boing, boing, boing*, every bounce making a sound like a plucked rubber band, and at the peak of each arc she'd unfold into girl-shape for a moment, wave at me, and then squish back down. Sometimes she rolled. At one point she poured herself along the top of a fence like a stream of melted candy. It was the most ridiculous thing I'd ever seen, and I had once seen my father try to assemble an IKEA bed.

"Stop following me!"

"But we're best friends!"

"We met ninety seconds ago!"

"Ninety *wonderful* seconds!" *Boing.* "What's your name? Mine is—" and here she made a sound, a sort of musical crystalline chiming that seemed to have harmonics in it, that made my teeth vibrate and my vision briefly turn into a kaleidoscope.

"I can't say that!"

"Then you pick!" *Boing.* "Give me a name! A friend-name!"

"I'm not naming you!"

It was a perfect sphere of rainbow liquid, and when it dripped off her chin it bounced on the pavement twice and then rolled back up her leg and reabsorbed into her body.

I am an average person. I have average defenses. I do not have the strength to withstand Puppy Eyes: Slime Edition.

"...Nijiko," I muttered.

Her colors flared back up so fast it was like a firework going off. "Nijiko?"

"Niji means rainbow. Ko is for a girl. Nijiko. Rainbow girl. It's not creative. Don't get excited."

"*NIJIKO!*" She threw her arms around me, and I was engulfed again, entirely, from head to knee, in warm sparkling jelly that fizzed against every inch of me. "I LOVE IT! I love it I love it I love it! I'm Nijiko! Mei-chan named me!"

"How do you know my name?!"

"It's on your bag!" She pointed a dripping finger at the little embroidered name tag my mother had sewn on in middle school and which I had never been able to remove because she'd used *industrial thread*.

We arrived at school four minutes late. The gate was being closed by Gouda-sensei, our PE teacher, a vast, square-jawed man built like a refrigerator wearing a tracksuit, who always had a whistle around his neck and a bamboo practice sword on his shoulder and the burning eyes of a man who had once almost gone to the Koshien baseball tournament and never got over it.

"No," I said.

"Yes!" said Nijiko.

"I see," said Gouda-sensei, in the tone of a man who had decided, for the sake of his own mental health, not to engage. "Get to the ceremony. Both of you."

They looked at her, they processed her, something in their brains short-circuited, and then they simply... accepted her, the way you accept weather. It was like the universe had a narrative immune system that forcibly smoothed over anything too strange.

Except for me. I got to experience the full strangeness. Every single second of it.

---

The opening ceremony was in the gymnasium. Six hundred students in neat rows of folding chairs, the principal droning at the podium about "the spring of your youth" and "the blossoming of your potential," and the faint smell of floor wax and nervous teenagers. I tried to sneak in at the back, hunched over, glittering faintly, praying to every god in the Shinto pantheon that no one would turn around.

Nijiko followed me in, and the stage lights hit her.

I don't think I can properly convey what happens when a powerful theater spotlight passes through a translucent, crystal-filled, rainbow-colored slime girl.
