I like Mei-chan, and pretty things, and Mei-chan, and eating! Nice to meet you!" She bowed deeply. Her head stretched toward the floor like taffy and then snapped back up. "Please take care of me!"

Thirty-two faces turned in perfect unison to look at me.

I have never wanted to die so much in my life. And I once called my homeroom teacher in middle school "Mom" in front of the entire class.

"Oh," said Mizuno-sensei faintly. "How... nice. Sato-san, please... help her... adjust."

"*Why me?!*"

"Because she's your best friend," said thirty-two people at once.

---

## Chapter Three: The Rooftop, the Tsundere, and the Otaku

At lunch, I fled to the roof.

The rooftop at Sakuragaoka is technically off-limits, which, in accordance with the sacred laws of fiction, means that the door is never locked and everyone goes up there. It's a wide, flat expanse of concrete surrounded by a tall green chain-link fence, with a water tank on one end and a view of the whole town: the river, the cherry trees, the distant blue hills, the cluttered tile roofs and the train line curving off toward the city.

I had been eating lunch up there with the same two people since our first year. They were my two best friends in the world. My *actual* best friends. The ones I had chosen, like a normal person, through years of gradual social bonding and shared embarrassments.

The first was Kirishima Kaede.

Kaede and I had been neighbors since we were four. She was taller than me, lean and athletic, the ace of the girls' kendo club, with a high, sharp ponytail of glossy black hair and narrow amber eyes and a perpetual scowl. She was rude. She was blunt. She was terrifyingly loyal. She had punched a boy in the third grade for pulling my hair and then immediately told me it was "not for you, idiot, he was just annoying."

She was, in other words, a textbook tsundere, and I loved her.

The second was Hoshino Ayumi, our class representative. Ayumi was small and round-faced, with thick braids and enormous glasses that reflected the light so you could never see her eyes when she was being dramatic, which was always. She was top of our year academically. She was also the single biggest anime and manga otaku I have ever met in my life. Her bag was covered in keychains. Her phone case was a limited-edition piece of merchandise from a magical girl show that had aired before we were born. She had once spent an entire lunch period explaining the thematic significance of a single frame of animation to me while I ate a melon bread in stunned silence.

They were already there, sitting on a blue picnic tarp by the fence, when I burst through the rooftop door, panting.

"Mei!" said Ayumi. "We heard!"

"*Everyone* heard," said Kaede, chopsticks halfway to her mouth. "There's a rumor going around the third-years that you summoned a demon in the gymnasium."

"I didn't summon anything! It fell on me!"

"What fell on you?"

The rooftop door, which I had slammed behind me, made a small squelching noise. Then Nijiko oozed under it. She flowed through the gap at the bottom like a spill of melted jewels, puddled on the concrete, and then rose up into her girl-shape, shaking herself like a wet dog and throwing off a spray of sparkles that hung in the air and slowly drifted down.

"Mei-chan! You left me! I almost got lost! A boy in the hallway tried to poke me with a pencil and I ate the pencil!"

"*You ate his pencil?*"

"It was yellow!" She patted her tummy. Floating inside her, slowly rotating among the crystals, was a perfectly intact HB pencil. As I watched, it began to glow faintly and fizz, and then dissolved into a shower of tiny yellow sparks.

Kaede dropped her chopsticks.

Ayumi's glasses flashed white. Pure, opaque white, like headlights. She rose slowly to her feet. Her braids seemed to lift slightly, as if from static electricity. Her hands were trembling.

"Is that," she whispered, "a *magical slime girl*?"

"No," I said.

"Yes!" said Nijiko.

Ayumi made a noise I have only ever heard from her once before, when she won a lottery for front-row tickets to a voice actor concert. It was a high, wavering, almost ultrasonic squeal, like a kettle achieving enlightenment.

"*KYAAAAAAAAAAH!*"

She lunged forward and grabbed Nijiko's hands. Nijiko, delighted, grabbed back, and Ayumi's hands sank into the jelly up to her wrists, and her glasses fogged up, and her face went bright red, and a thin trickle of blood ran from her left nostril.

"Ayumi! Your nose!"

"I'm *fine*," she said, with the serene voice of a woman ascending to heaven. "Mei. Mei. Do you understand what's happening to you? A mysterious magical creature has descended from the sky and imprinted on you, an average schoolgirl, on the first day of the new term. This is the inciting incident! You're the *protagonist*! This is the first episode! There's going to be an opening theme song!"

"There is not going to be an opening theme song."

From somewhere I swear I heard a faint, peppy synthesizer riff. I looked around wildly. It stopped.

Kaede, meanwhile, had not moved. She sat on the tarp, her bento on her lap, staring at Nijiko with an expression of deep, simmering, profound suspicion. Her hand had drifted toward the bamboo sword in its bag beside her.

"Mei," she said, very evenly. "Why is it calling you 'Mei-chan.'"

"I don't know! It's been doing that all morning!"

"Because Mei-chan is my best friend!" Nijiko declared, beaming.

The temperature on the rooftop dropped about five degrees. A small storm cloud of pure dark aura appeared over Kaede's head. I am not being metaphorical. I could actually see it, a little scribble of black, crackling with tiny lightning.

"Best," said Kaede, "friend."

"Yup!"

"*I'm* her best friend."

"Okay!" said Nijiko happily. "Then we can both be best friends! A best-friend team! Like a sentai!"

"That's not how it works!"

"Why not?"

Kaede opened her mouth. Closed it. Opened it again. A dull red flush crept up her neck. She turned her head sharply away, ponytail whipping.

"I-it's not like I care who Mei's best friend is or anything!" she snapped. "She can be friends with whatever weird glowing jelly she wants! It doesn't matter to me *at all*! Hmph!"

Ayumi took a reverent photo with her phone. "Perfect tsundere response," she murmured. "Textbook. I'm going to frame this."

"*Delete that!*"

---

We ate lunch together. All four of us. I didn't have a choice.

Nijiko, it turned out, was extremely interested in food. She sat beside me, pressed against my side so that half my blazer was glittering, and watched me open my bento with her enormous starry eyes fixed on it like I was unveiling a treasure.

My mother had made me rice with a pickled plum in the middle, tamagoyaki, two little octopus-shaped sausages, broccoli, and a single cherry tomato. It was a normal bento. An average bento.

"What's that?" asked Nijiko, pointing at the octopus sausage.

"It's a sausage. Cut to look like an octopus."

"*Why?*"

"...Because it's cute?"

Nijiko gasped like I had told her the meaning of life. "Humans make food *cute*? On *purpose*? Just because?"

"I... guess?"

"Can I try it?"

I sighed and held it out on my chopsticks. Nijiko leaned forward and *swallowed it whole, chopsticks and all*. The ends of my chopsticks vanished into her face. I yanked them back. They came out clean, polished, and faintly sparkling. Inside her, the little octopus sausage floated down to rest near her heart crystal, tumbling slowly. The crystal pulsed pink. Then the sausage began to glow, and fizz, and, in a flash of light and a sound like a tiny chime, it dissolved into a burst of *pink, octopus-shaped sparkles* that drifted up through her body and out the top of her head like bubbles in champagne.

Her whole body flushed rose-gold. She put her hands on her cheeks. Her eyes went watery with joy.

"*It tastes like love,*" she whispered.

"It tastes like a sausage!"

"Mei-chan's mother made it with love! I can taste it! It's all warm and fuzzy and soft and it says 'please do your best today, Mei'!"

I went very quiet.

My mother did, in fact, say exactly that to me every morning. "Please do your best today, Mei." I'd never thought about it as something she put into the food.

Kaede, sulking, held out one of her own tamagoyaki on her chopsticks, not looking at Nijiko, her face still red. "...Here. Try mine. Just to compare. Not because I want you to like it or anything."

Nijiko ate it. And the chopsticks. And for one brief, terrible moment, most of Kaede's hand.

"KYAA! LET GO! LET GO OF MY HAND!"

"Sorry!" Nijiko spat her hand back out. It was perfectly fine, just glittery to the elbow. "Your egg tastes like *trying really hard*! And like you got up early and burned the first one and threw it out and made it again! And you're a little bit embarrassed about it!"

Kaede's face went from red to crimson to a deep, rich shade of purple. Steam came out of her ears. Actual steam.

"*I DID NOT BURN THE FIRST ONE!*"

"You burned the first two," said Ayumi, not looking up from her phone. "Your mom posted about it on her blog."

---

## Chapter Four: Physical Education, or, the Day Nijiko Ate the Pool

I want to say that things settled down after the first day.

They did not.

Every morning, Nijiko was waiting for me outside my front door, glittering on the doorstep like an enormous, sentient jewel. She had decided that she lived there now. She slept, as far as I could tell, in the koi pond in our garden, which my father was initially very upset about until he noticed that his koi had started glowing faintly in the dark and seemed extremely happy. My mother had taken one look at her on the first evening, blinked twice, and said, "Oh, Mei, you made a friend! Would she like some dinner?" and that was the end of the discussion. My little brother Souta, who is nine, thought Nijiko was the coolest thing that had ever happened to our family. He'd taught her to play video games. She was terrifyingly good at them. She could hold three controllers at once.

At school, people were starting to recognize me. Not as "Sato Mei." As "the slime girl's friend." People whispered when I walked down the hallway. First-years asked for my autograph. Someone started a fan account. It had eleven hundred followers. It was mostly blurry photos of Nijiko eating things that weren't food.

And then there was PE.

In the second week of term, Gouda-sensei announced, with the fire of a thousand suns, that we would be starting swimming early this year, because the pool heater had been fixed, and because "THE WATER IS WHERE THE SPIRIT OF YOUTH IS TESTED!"

I have mixed feelings about swim class. I don't like the regulation school swimsuit. It's dark navy and has a little white name tag sewn on the front, and nobody looks good in it, except Kaede, who looks good in everything because she has the body of a competitive athlete and doesn't even care. I'm an okay swimmer. Average. I can do about twenty-five meters of freestyle before I start swallowing water.

Nijiko had never seen a pool before.

We came out of the changing rooms, all of us girls in Class 2-B, shivering a little in the April air, and filed onto the wet tiles beside the school's outdoor pool. It was a big, clean, chlorine-blue rectangle, eight lanes wide, gleaming in the sun. Nijiko came out of the changing room behind me. She had shaped herself a swimsuit. It was a perfect replica of the school swimsuit, except that it was made of her own jelly, sparkling and translucent and shifting in color, and the little name tag on the front said **NIJIKO** in wobbly bubble letters that floated just above the surface of her chest.

She looked at the pool.

Her eyes got bigger. And bigger. And *bigger*. The stars in them multiplied and began to spin.

"Mei-chan," she whispered. "It's a *giant* bowl of *sparkly water*."

"Nijiko, no—"

"*It's so pretty!*"

"Nijiko, wait for Gouda-sensei's whistle—"

She jumped in.

It was not a dive. It was not a cannonball. It was more like she *poured* herself from the edge into the water, all at once, like someone tipping a bucket of rainbow paint into the pool. And the moment she touched the water, she *spread*.

The entire pool, all eight lanes, changed color. A wave of brilliant rainbow swept from one end to the other, like a sunrise rushing across the surface. The water turned thick, shimmering, iridescent. Crystals bloomed in it, little faceted gems sprouting up everywhere, catching the sun, throwing light across the faces of thirty shocked high school girls. Sparks crackled across the surface in long, beautiful forks, like tiny harmless lightning. Glitter rose from it in a soft, glowing mist.

The pool had become a giant, glowing, sparkling jelly. It wobbled gently in the breeze.

And somewhere in the middle of it, two enormous violet eyes opened.

"*Mei-chan!*" boomed the pool, in Nijiko's voice, magnified a hundred times, chiming like a cathedral bell. "*I'm SO BIG! LOOK AT ME!*"

Gouda-sensei stood at the edge of the pool, whistle halfway to his lips. His face was utterly blank. A single vein pulsed in his forehead.

He lowered the whistle. He looked at the sky for a long time.

"...Free period," he said finally. "Everyone. Free period. I need to go lie down."

He walked away very slowly, like a man walking away from an explosion.

The class stood there in silence for a moment. Then Takahashi from the volleyball club jumped in. She landed in the jelly with a soft *bloop*, bounced, and came up laughing, coated head to toe in glitter, glowing faintly. "IT'S SO SOFT!" she screamed. "IT'S LIKE A WATERBED MADE OF CANDY!"

Then *everyone* jumped in.

It became, I am sorry to say, the single greatest PE class in Sakuragaoka history. Girls bouncing and sliding and laughing, the pool rippling with rainbow light, Nijiko making little crystal slides and gentle waves and blowing big glittering bubbles that drifted up into the air and popped into showers of sparks. Even Kaede joined in, eventually, though she pretended she'd "slipped." Ayumi floated on her back in the middle, her glasses perfectly fogged, murmuring "*This is the swimsuit episode. This is the swimsuit episode*" over and over like a prayer.

I stayed at the edge.

I sat with my arms around my knees, in my navy swimsuit, watching everyone, and I felt... strange. Hot-faced and uncomfortable and squirmy inside. Everyone was laughing. Everyone was having fun. And it was all because of *her*, because of the strange, impossible, sparkling thing that had attached herself to me, and everyone was looking at her and then looking at me and I was supposed to be *invisible*. I was supposed to be *background*. I'd spent my whole life learning how to be background.

A wave of jelly lapped up against my feet. It touched me gently, curling around my toes. Warm and fizzy.

"*Mei-chan,*" said the pool, softly, just to me. "*Aren't you coming in?*"

"I'm fine here," I muttered.

The pool was quiet for a moment.

"*Okay,*" said Nijiko. And she didn't push. She just stayed there, curled around my toes, warm and glowing, for the rest of the period. Like she was holding my hand.

---

## Chapter Five: Ohohoho! The Student Council President Declares War

Of course there was a student council president. Of course she was rich. Of course she had drill hair.

Her name was Himemiya Reika, and she was a third-year, and she was the daughter of the CEO of Himemiya Heavy Industries, and she had long, golden-blonde hair arranged into four enormous, gravity-defying, perfectly spiraled ringlets. She wore the same uniform as everyone else, but somehow on her it looked like haute couture. She carried a folding fan made of white lace. She had two personal attendants, both second-year girls from Class 2-A, who followed her around and threw rose petals. I have no idea where they got the rose petals. It was a total mystery to everyone.

She found us in the courtyard during lunch at the beginning of the third week, where I was trying to eat a melon bread in peace while Nijiko sat beside me on a bench, slowly absorbing a can of melon soda, can and all, and making happy little fizzing sounds.

"*Ohohohoho!*"

The laugh came from everywhere at once. It echoed off the school buildings. Rose petals fluttered down from above. I looked up and saw Himemiya Reika descending the courtyard steps, fan pressed to her lips, drills bouncing, attendants flanking her and flinging petals with wild abandon.

"So *you're* the one," she said, sweeping to a stop in front of us and snapping her fan shut to point at Nijiko. "The so-called 'Rainbow Miracle of Sakuragaoka.' The girl whose fan account has twelve thousand followers. *Twelve thousand!* *Mine* only has *eleven thousand eight hundred!*"

"Hello!" said Nijiko, with her mouth full of soda can. "You have pretty hair! It's all twirly! Like a seashell!"

Himemiya faltered for a fraction of a second. A small pink blush appeared on her cheeks. "W-well, *naturally*. My hairdresser comes in from Paris twice a week." She regained her composure with a flick of her fan. "Regardless! The Sakuragaoka Culture Festival is in six weeks. The student council has always run the most popular attraction. It is *tradition*. It is my *birthright*. And I will not be outshone by a... by a... *glittery dessert!*"

"I'm not a dessert!" said Nijiko. She paused. She looked down at herself thoughtfully. "...Am I a dessert?"

"You're not a dessert," I said wearily.

"*Ohohoho!* Then I challenge you! Class 2-B against the student council! Whichever attraction draws the most visitors at the culture festival wins! And if *I* win..." She pointed her fan dramatically at me. "...the slime girl will join the *student council*!"

"Okay!" said Nijiko.

"*WAIT—*" I said.

"And if *you* win," Himemiya continued, ignoring me, "I'll give you... *anything you want!*"

"Can I have a ride in your car?" said Nijiko.

"...My car?"

"It's long and shiny and white! I saw it this morning! It looked like a big marshmallow!"

Himemiya stared at her. Her attendants stopped throwing petals. She cleared her throat. "That is my *limousine*. It is imported from Germany. It has a minibar and a massage chair and a small aquarium."

"*An aquarium!*" Nijiko gasped.

"...Yes, very well," said Himemiya, looking deeply thrown. "Fine. If you win, you may ride in my limousine. *Ohohohoho!*" And she turned and swept away, petals flying, drills bouncing, leaving me sitting in the courtyard holding a half-eaten melon bread and wondering at what point my life had gone so wrong.

"Mei-chan," said Nijiko, swallowing the last of her soda can with a satisfied sparkle. "What's a culture festival?"

---

## Chapter Six: Kurosawa-senpai

Here is a secret I had never told anyone. Not even Kaede. Not even Ayumi, who would have screamed and made a shrine about it.

I had a crush on Kurosawa-senpai.

Kurosawa Ren was a third-year. He was the president of the literature club, which I had joined in my first year for no reason at all, absolutely not because I'd seen him reading in the library on the day of club recruitment and fallen so deeply and completely in love that I'd walked into a bookshelf. He was tall and slim and quiet, with slightly messy black hair that fell into his gray eyes, and he had long, pale hands that he used to turn the pages of old poetry books with tremendous care. He wore his uniform a little loose, the top button undone. He smelled like old paper and green tea. He spoke very softly and very rarely, and when he did, it was always something kind or clever or both.

He had spoken directly to me exactly seven times in a full year. I remembered every single one. The best one was when I had dropped my pen in the clubroom and he had picked it up and handed it back to me and said "Here," and our fingers had *touched*, very briefly, and I'd gone home and lain on my bed and screamed into a pillow for twenty minutes.

He was my *Rintarou-sama*. He was the reason I read shoujo manga. He was the reason I wanted, more than anything, to be quiet and gentle and pretty and normal. Because if I was quiet and gentle and pretty and normal, someday, maybe, under the legendary cherry tree behind the school, he might look at me and...

Anyway.

The point is that I had very carefully, very deliberately, *not* brought Nijiko to the literature club.

I had told her it was a very boring club where people sat quietly and read old books and no one ate anything ever. I had told her it was dangerous for slimes. I had implied, possibly, that the books were poisonous.

So when I opened the door to the literature clubroom on a quiet Thursday afternoon in the fourth week of term, and found Nijiko sitting cross-legged on the long wooden table, holding an ancient leather-bound collection of classical tanka poetry, with Kurosawa-senpai sitting across from her, *smiling*...

I froze in the doorway.

The clubroom was golden with late-afternoon sun. Dust floated in it like pollen. Nijiko's crystals caught the slanting light and threw rainbows across the bookshelves, across the faded spines of a hundred old books, across Kurosawa-senpai's face, so that his gray eyes reflected little points of pink and blue and gold. He was leaning on his elbow. He looked... *amused*. Happy, even. I'd never seen him look like that.

"...and so the poet is saying that even though the moon is the same moon, it looks different because his heart is different," he was saying, softly. "Because the person he loved isn't there to see it with him anymore."

Nijiko's eyes were huge and wet. Her colors had gone soft and blue and silver, like twilight. "That's so sad," she whispered. "But it's so pretty. Why do humans make sad things pretty?"

Kurosawa-senpai considered this. "I think," he said, "it's so we can bear them."

Nijiko sniffled. A rainbow tear bounced across the table.

Then she looked up and saw me in the doorway. Her whole body lit up like a Christmas tree.

"*MEI-CHAN!* You were *wrong*! The books aren't *poisonous*! Senpai has been reading them to me and they're all about love and the moon and people being sad in pretty ways! And they taste like *dust* and *old ink* and *someone crying a long time ago*!"

My face went *hot*. So hot I'm surprised my hair didn't catch fire. Kurosawa-senpai turned to look at me. He was still smiling. My heart did a thing it had never done before, a kind of triple flip with a twist.

"Sato-san," he said. My *name*. He knew my *name*. "Your friend is very interesting. She said you told her the books were poisonous."

"I—I—I—" I said intelligently.

"She asked me why the moon in this poem was lonely," he said. "I've read that poem a hundred times. I never thought to ask that." He smiled down at the page. "It was a good question."

And then he looked back up at me, and he said, gently, "You're lucky, to have a friend like that."

I stood there. My mouth opened and closed. Steam was definitely coming out of my ears. Nijiko was waving at me with both arms, sparkling, and Kurosawa-senpai was smiling at me, and the golden light was pouring through the window, and it was *exactly* like a scene from *Kiss Me Under the Starlit Greenhouse*, except that the most important person in the scene was not me. It was the glittering jelly girl on the table.

Of course it was.

"Excuse me," I squeaked. And I turned and fled, and the door banged shut behind me, and I ran all the way down the stairs and out of the building and didn't stop until I was halfway home, gasping, my eyes stinging for a reason I couldn't name.

## Chapter Seven: The Culture Festival

Class 2-B decided, by an overwhelming majority vote, to run a maid café.

I voted for a quiet exhibition about the history of our town. I was the only one.

"A *maid café*!" said Ayumi, standing at the blackboard with chalk in hand, glasses gleaming with determination. "But not just *any* maid café! A *magical starlight maid café*! With Nijiko as the centerpiece! She can do the lighting! The decorations! The special effects! We'll have rainbow parfaits and sparkling drinks and—"

"Rainbow parfaits?" said Nijiko, with the reverent voice of a pilgrim. "Can I eat them?"

"You can *make* them," said Ayumi. "And then *other* people eat them."

Nijiko looked like she was having a crisis of faith.

For five weeks, Class 2-B transformed itself. Everyone worked. Desks were pushed together and covered in lace tablecloths sewn by the handicrafts club girls. Paper stars were cut out by the hundreds. Takahashi from volleyball and her friends painted a giant mural of a night sky on rolls of paper and hung it from the ceiling. Kaede, grumbling, built a little stage out of plywood with a hammer and the expression of a woman avenging a murder. Ayumi designed the maid uniforms herself: pastel blue and pink dresses with puffy sleeves and white aprons and little star-shaped hair ribbons. Every single one of them was perfect. She did not sleep for nine days.

And Nijiko... Nijiko was *everywhere*.

She learned, under Ayumi's frantic instruction, how to make rainbow parfaits. She would stand behind the counter in a tiny maid outfit she'd formed out of herself, and she would hold a parfait glass, and she would close her eyes and hum, and colored jelly would flow from her fingertips into the glass in perfect layers: strawberry, mango, lime, blueberry, grape, swirling and settling into neat bands, and then she would sprinkle it with tiny edible crystals, real crystallized sugar that she *grew from her own palms*, glittering and sweet. Ayumi tested one, took one bite, and fell over backward in a dead faint, smiling.

She learned how to do the lighting. In the evenings, after the rest of the class went home, we'd stay behind, me and Nijiko, and she'd practice. She'd spread herself thin across the ceiling like a stained-glass window, and the late sun would shine through her, and the whole classroom would fill with dancing rainbow light, swirling and wheeling, shapes of stars and moons and flowers drifting across the walls. It was the most beautiful thing I'd ever seen.

I never told her that.

I watched from the doorway, every evening. I watched her work. I watched the class love her. I watched Kurosawa-senpai stop by on his way home, two or three times, and lean on the doorframe and watch her with a little smile, and say "Good work, Nijiko-san," and once, when she made the light into the shape of the lonely moon from the poem, he'd laughed out loud, a soft surprised sound I'd never heard before, and something in my chest had *hurt*.

I didn't understand it. I didn't want to understand it. I just felt it, every day, a little sharp, hot ache, getting worse.

---

The culture festival came on a Saturday in late May, warm and clear and blue.

The whole school was transformed. Colorful banners hung from every window. Paper lanterns were strung across the courtyard. The smell of takoyaki and yakisoba and cotton candy drifted from food stalls run by the sports clubs. The brass band played on the front steps. The drama club performed a version of *Romeo and Juliet* in which Juliet was played by a very tall boy from the rugby team, and he was magnificent. The halls were packed with students, parents, younger siblings, kids from other schools, old graduates coming back to visit.

And the line for Class 2-B's Magical Starlight Maid Café went all the way down the corridor, down two flights of stairs, out the front door, and halfway around the courtyard.

The student council, it was later revealed, had built a full-scale replica of a European palace ballroom in the gymnasium, with an orchestra, imported chandeliers, and a chocolate fountain three meters high. Himemiya Reika stood at the gymnasium doors greeting guests in a gold ball gown, drills magnificently coiffed, laughing *ohohoho* every thirty seconds. It was spectacular. It was decadent. It was *empty*, because everyone was in line for us.

Inside our classroom, it was magic. I don't have another word for it.

Nijiko had spread herself across the entire ceiling, thin as a soap bubble, and the light from the windows poured through her and filled the room with shifting, glowing color, like being inside a kaleidoscope. Stars glittered on the walls. Crystals hung from the ceiling, growing like icicles, catching the light and refracting it into little dancing rainbows that swam across the guests' faces and hands. Every few minutes, a gentle shower of sparkles would drift down from above, harmless and cool, landing on people's hair and shoulders and melting into faint, glowing glitter.

And at the center of the room, on Kaede's little plywood stage, a second, smaller Nijiko—she had *split herself*, somehow, a thing I'd never seen her do—stood in her maid outfit, making rainbow parfaits, and singing.

She sang a song with no words, in that wind-chime ramune-bottle voice, a melody that seemed to rise and fall like waves, and the light in the room pulsed along with it. Little kids sat in front of the stage, open-mouthed, staring. Grown adults wiped their eyes. A visiting grandmother asked if she could take Nijiko home.

I was in a maid uniform too. Pale blue. Puffy sleeves. A little star ribbon in my hair. Ayumi had insisted. I was carrying trays of parfaits back and forth, trying to be invisible, and failing, because everyone who came in the door looked at the singing slime girl and then looked around the room, and the first thing they asked was, "Which one of you is Mei-chan?"

Because she kept *saying* it. Every song she sang, every parfait she made, every wave and twirl and sparkle, she would shout it out: "*This one's for Mei-chan!*" "*Mei-chan, look!*" "*Mei-chan is my best friend in the whole wide universe!*"

And every time, every single time, every face in the room would turn to look at me.

My face was red all day long. My ears were burning. I kept my eyes down. I carried my trays. I told myself it would be over soon.

And then, at three in the afternoon, Kurosawa-senpai came in.

He was alone. He was wearing his uniform, a little loose, the top button undone. He stood in the doorway in the rainbow light and looked around the room, and he found me, standing by the counter in my pale blue maid uniform with a tray in my hands.

He smiled at me.

He started walking toward me.

My heart stopped. Everything stopped. The noise of the room faded to nothing. He was coming toward me through the swirling rainbow light, his gray eyes catching flecks of color, and he was smiling, and I was in a cute uniform, and this was it, this was *the scene*, the scene I'd been dreaming of since the first day I'd walked into a bookshelf—

"*MEI-CHAAAAN!*"

Nijiko, the stage-Nijiko, had seen him. She'd seen him walking toward me. She'd seen my face, which must have been bright red. And Nijiko, who was made of starlight and happiness and something called quantum jelly, who loved pretty things, who'd cried over a poem about a lonely moon, decided, in that moment, with all the love in her sparkling heart, to *help*.

She leapt off the stage. Mid-leap she expanded, gathered up her ceiling-self, poured it all back into herself in a single rushing wave of light that made the whole room flicker. She landed between me and Kurosawa-senpai, three times her normal size, a glowing, towering pillar of rainbow jelly, and she threw out her arms, and she shouted, at the top of her bell-like voice, so loud it echoed through the whole floor of the building—

"*SENPAI! MEI-CHAN LIKES YOU! SHE'S LIKED YOU FOR A WHOLE YEAR! SHE WRITES YOUR NAME IN THE BACK OF HER NOTEBOOK AND THEN SCRIBBLES IT OUT! SHE WALKED INTO A BOOKSHELF BECAUSE OF YOU! SHE SAYS 'GOODNIGHT, RINTAROU-SAMA' TO HER MANGA BUT I THINK SHE MEANS YOU! PLEASE GO OUT WITH HER! SHE'S THE BEST GIRL IN THE WHOLE UNIVERSE!*"

And then she exploded into a shower of glittering heart-shaped sparkles that rained down over everyone and everything, a pink and red and gold confetti storm of pure, radiant, unbearable *love*.

The room was silent.

A hundred people stared at me.

Kurosawa-senpai stood in the falling hearts, a sparkle stuck in his messy hair, his gray eyes wide, his lips slightly parted.

Ayumi, across the room, dropped her phone.

Kaede, by the door, put her face in her hands.

I stood there holding my tray. My face had gone past red. It had gone past crimson. It had reached a temperature not previously observed in nature. I could feel every single eye on me. I could feel my heartbeat in my eyeballs. I could feel a year of careful, quiet, secret hoping, crumpled up and thrown into the street and run over by a truck.

The tray slipped out of my hands and fell, and three rainbow parfaits smashed on the floor in a splash of color and crystal and glass.

"*Why,*" I said. My voice came out tiny and strange and cracked. "Why would you *do* that?"

Nijiko, reforming in front of me, small again, girl-sized, looked at me with her huge starry eyes. Her colors were flickering uncertainly. "B-because you were so red, Mei-chan. And you looked so happy and so scared. And I thought—I thought if he knew, then—"

"*You don't think!*" It burst out of me. All of it. Five weeks of it, five weeks of watching the whole world fall in love with her, five weeks of hot aching jealousy I had refused to name, a whole lifetime of trying to be invisible. "You *never* think! You just—you just *happen* to people! You fell on my face! You followed me to school! You told the whole class we were best friends! You ate the pool! You ate Senpai's *books*! Everyone looks at me now! Everyone *knows* me now! I was *fine*! I was *normal*! I was *happy* being nobody and you *ruined it*! I never asked for you! I never *wanted* you! I wish you'd fallen on *somebody else!*"

The words rang in the silent room.

I watched them hit her.

I watched her colors drain.

It started at the edges, at the tips of her dripping, rainbow hair. The rose and tangerine, the mint and sapphire, faded, washed out, went pale and gray, like a photograph left in the sun. The paleness crept inward, through her shoulders, her arms, her chest. The sparkles around her went out one by one, like stars at dawn. The crystals inside her dimmed. And the heart, the plum-sized rose-gold heart crystal at the center of her chest, flickered, and flickered, and went dark.

She stood there, gray and translucent and hollow-looking, like a ghost of herself. Like a glass of water.

"...Okay," she said, in a very small voice. It didn't sound like wind chimes anymore. It just sounded quiet. "Sorry, Mei-chan."

And she melted. Right there, in front of everyone. She collapsed into a small, gray, dull puddle on the classroom floor, and she slid away, across the floorboards, out the door, through the forest of legs in the hallway, and was gone.

---

## Chapter Eight: Rain

It started to rain at five o'clock.

The sky had been perfectly blue all day, and then, in a single hour, clouds piled up out of nowhere: huge, dark, purple-gray thunderheads that came boiling over the hills and swallowed the sun. The first drops fell fat and cold. Then it poured. The culture festival was cut short, stalls hurriedly packed away, lanterns taken down, parents and visitors fleeing to their cars under umbrellas.

Of course it rained. It *always* rains in the scene after the protagonist says something terrible. I knew that. I'd read it a hundred times.

It's different when it happens to you.

I stood in the empty classroom, still in my maid uniform, surrounded by the wreckage of the café. The paper stars had come loose and fallen. The night sky mural was peeling. Without Nijiko's light, the whole room looked cheap and gray, just a classroom with some lace tablecloths and bits of glitter scattered on the floor. The parfait I'd dropped was still there, a smear of color on the boards. Someone had swept up the glass.

Kaede stood beside me. Ayumi sat in a chair, her glasses off, rubbing her eyes. Neither of them had said anything for a long time.

Kurosawa-senpai had left. He'd looked at me for a long moment, after Nijiko vanished, with an expression I couldn't read, and then he'd turned and gone, quietly. I didn't know what that meant. I found, to my own surprise, that I didn't really care.

"Say something," I said at last. My voice was hoarse. "Tell me I'm a terrible person. Go ahead."

Kaede looked at me. Her amber eyes were very serious. For once, there was no blush, no scowl, no stammering denial.

"You're not a terrible person, Mei," she said. "You're an *idiot*. That's different."

Ayumi put her glasses back on. They didn't flash. They were just glasses. Behind them, her eyes were red. "She loves you so much, Mei," she said quietly. "You know that, right? The way she looks at you. She never looks at anyone else like that. Not even Senpai. She only ever liked Senpai because she could tell you did."

I looked down at my hands.

On the backs of them, faintly, even now, there was a little glitter. There was always glitter. I'd been scrubbing it off in the bath for seven weeks and it never all came off. I'd stopped noticing. And I realized, standing there in the gray, empty room, that I didn't want it to come off. That I'd gotten *used* to it. Used to the warm, fizzy weight of her pressed against my side at lunch. Used to waking up to a sparkling girl waving at me through my bedroom window from the koi pond. Used to the octopus-shaped sparkles that came out of her head when she ate my mother's sausages. Used to the sound of her saying my name like it was the best word she'd ever learned.

*It tastes like love*, she'd said.

I'd been so busy being embarrassed that I'd never once said thank you.

"I have to find her," I said.

"Yeah," said Kaede. "No kidding."

---

We searched everywhere.

The three of us ran through the rain, through the emptying school, calling her name. "*NIJIKO!*" Through the dark hallways, through the gymnasium where Himemiya's ballroom was being dismantled, where Himemiya herself, still in her gold gown, hair drills slightly drooping in the humidity, asked us what was wrong, and when we told her, she snapped her fan shut and said, "*Ohoho*—no. No laughing. Not now. Attendants! Search the east wing!" and her two attendants ran off, flinging rose petals in a panic.

We searched the literature clubroom. Empty. The poetry book lay open on the table at the page about the lonely moon.

We searched the pool. It was just a pool. Blue and cold and rain-spattered, and so ordinary it hurt.

Gouda-sensei found us in the courtyard, soaked to the skin, and when we explained, his face went grim and fierce and he said, "*SATO!* A friend in need is the TRUE TEST OF YOUTH!" and blew his whistle so hard the rain seemed to stop for a second, and then he got on his phone and called the entire baseball team, who arrived eleven minutes later with flashlights and enormous determination.

Mizuno-sensei searched the faculty room, her glasses fogged. My mother arrived with umbrellas and my little brother Souta, who was crying because "*Nijiko-nee-chan promised to show me her final form!*"

By the time the sun had gone down entirely, half of Sakuragaoka High was out in the rain, searching for a gray puddle the size of a teenage girl.

And it was me, in the end, who found her.

Because I knew. Somewhere, deep down, I'd known all along where she'd go. It was where she'd *started*.

---

I ran out of the school gates, down the street, across the road, and onto the river embankment.

The rain was coming down in sheets. The river was swollen and dark, roaring along between its banks. The cherry trees stood in a long row, black against the purple sky, their branches bare now, the blossoms long fallen, just green leaves shuddering in the wind. The path was muddy. My maid uniform was soaked through and clinging to me, the puffy sleeves collapsed, the star ribbon dripping. I'd lost a shoe somewhere. I didn't care.

I found the tree. The one she'd fallen out of. I'd walked past it every day for seven weeks, and every day she'd waved at it and said "Good morning, tree!" and I'd rolled my eyes.

She was curled up at its roots.

She was so small. Smaller than I'd ever seen her. Just a little gray lump, no bigger than a cat, huddled in the mud between two roots, half-hidden by fallen leaves. The rain drummed on her, and every drop that hit her seemed to wash a little bit more of her away. She was thin and watery and colorless, like a jellyfish washed up on a beach. Barely there.

Inside her, at the very center, I could just make out the heart crystal. It wasn't glowing. It was gray and cloudy, like a frosted window. And it was cracked. A thin, jagged line ran right across it.

"*Nijiko!*"

I fell to my knees in the mud beside her. I scooped her up. She was cold. She'd never been cold before. She was always cool, like a peach from the fridge, but never cold, never like this, like the rain itself, like something that was giving up.

She stirred, very faintly, in my hands. Two eyes opened in the gray. They were dull. No stars at all.

"...Mei-chan?" Barely a whisper. "Why are you here? You're getting wet."

"*I don't care!*" I was crying. I didn't even notice when I'd started. The tears were hot on my face, hot against the cold rain. "I don't care, I don't care, Nijiko, I'm so sorry, I'm so so sorry—"

"It's okay," she whispered. "You were right. I don't think. I just... happen. I fell on you and I didn't ask. I'm sorry I made everyone look at you. I just wanted... everyone to see how wonderful you are. Because you are. You're so wonderful, Mei-chan. You just don't believe it." Her gray body trembled. "I'll go back up. Back to the stars. It's okay. You can be normal again. I'll fall on someone else next time."

"*No!*"

I pulled her close. I held her against my chest, against my heart, wrapped both arms around her, bent over her in the mud to shield her from the rain. She was so cold. I pressed my face into her.

"No, no, no, you *can't*. You can't fall on someone else. You're *mine*. You're my best friend. You hear me? You're my *best friend*. I'm sorry I said those things. I didn't mean them. I was jealous, okay? I was *jealous*! Because everyone loves you, and you're so bright and brave and you just *say* things, and you make people *happy*, and I could never, I've never—I've spent my whole life trying to be invisible because I was so scared, and you came along and you just *saw* me, you saw me from the very first second, nobody's ever *seen* me like that, and I was so scared of it that I hurt you, and I'm *sorry*—"

I was babbling. I didn't care. Snot and tears and rain all running down my face.

"You made my life *loud*," I sobbed. "You made it *bright*. You made it so *embarrassing*, Nijiko, you have *no idea* how embarrassing, every single day, and I—I *love* it. I love it. Please don't go. Please. I'll let you sit next to me at lunch forever. I'll share my octopus sausages. I'll take you to every pool in Japan. I'll let you tell Senpai anything you want. I don't even care about Senpai. I care about *you*. Please stay. *Please stay with me.*"

The rain fell.

The river roared.

And then, against my chest, very faintly, something went *pchk*.

A tiny spark. Pink. It jumped from her body to my wrist, and fizzed.

Then another. *Pchk.* Blue.

I lifted my face. In my arms, the gray lump was *glowing*. Just barely. A faint, warm, rose-gold light was kindling deep inside her, at the very center, in the cracked heart crystal. As I watched, the crack began to fill with light, like gold flowing into a broken bowl. *Kintsugi*, my grandmother had called it, when she'd shown me the old tea bowl she'd repaired that way. *The break is part of its history. It's more beautiful for having been broken.*

The light spread.

It flowed out from her heart through her whole body, and with it came the colors, all of them, rushing back, *pouring* back, rose and tangerine and mint and sapphire and lemon and lilac, brighter than before, so bright they lit up the rain around us so that every falling drop became a tiny glittering prism. The crystals inside her blazed back to life one by one, a hundred, a thousand, a constellation. Sparks crackled out across her surface in great joyous forks and leapt from her to me and back again, wrapping around us both in a cage of harmless, dancing, electric light. Her body swelled and grew and rose and gathered itself, back into a girl, a girl kneeling in the mud in front of me, holding my hands, glowing like a sunrise.

Her eyes opened.

The stars were back. More of them than ever. Whole galaxies, spinning.

"*Mei-chan,*" she breathed, and her voice was wind chimes and ramune bottles and laughter again. "You said I'm your best friend."

"You *are* my best friend."

"You said it *out loud*."

"I know."

"*In front of the tree!*"

"I *know!*"

She threw her arms around me.

And she exploded.

Not in a bad way. In the *best* way. A column of light shot up from where we knelt, straight up into the storm, a pillar of pure rainbow brilliance that pierced the clouds like a spear. Light rolled out from it in a great ring, a shockwave of color that swept across the river, across the embankment, across the whole town. Where it touched the clouds, they *broke*. They parted. They peeled back like curtains, and behind them was the night sky, clear and deep and black, crowded with stars.

And then the light reached the cherry trees.

Every tree along the embankment, the whole long row of them, a hundred trees stretching off into the night, *burst into bloom*. In late May. Weeks after the blossoms had fallen. But they bloomed, all at once, with a sound like a breath being let out, and the blossoms weren't pink. They were *every* color. Rainbow blossoms, glowing faintly, translucent and crystalline, glittering with light, every petal shimmering with its own little spark. They glowed in the darkness like lanterns. And then a wind came, soft and warm, and the petals lifted off the branches all at once and swirled up into the air, a hundred thousand of them, a great luminous storm of rainbow cherry blossoms dancing over the river under the stars.

I stared up at it with my mouth open, my wet hair plastered to my face, Nijiko's arms around my neck.

Behind us, on the road, there were voices. I turned my head.

They were all there.

Kaede, soaking wet, her ponytail dripping, her hand over her mouth. Ayumi beside her, glasses flashing pure white, tears streaming from beneath them, holding up her phone with a trembling hand. Himemiya Reika in her gold gown, which was ruined, her drills completely collapsed into wet, waving blonde hair, staring upward with her lips parted and her fan forgotten in her hand. Her attendants had run out of rose petals. They didn't need them. Gouda-sensei and the entire baseball team, flashlights pointed uselessly at the ground, every single one of them sobbing openly. Mizuno-sensei, her glasses completely fogged. My mother, holding Souta, both of them smiling. Takahashi from volleyball and half of Class 2-B. Students. Teachers. Neighbors who had come out of their houses in their pajamas, holding umbrellas they'd forgotten to open.

And at the very back, standing a little apart, Kurosawa-senpai, his face tilted up to the falling glowing petals, a quiet look of wonder on it. He caught my eye. He smiled, small and warm. Then he looked at Nijiko, still wrapped around my neck, glowing, and he nodded to me, just slightly, like he understood. Like he'd understood since the clubroom. *You're lucky, to have a friend like that.*

He had been right.

"Mei-chan," Nijiko whispered in my ear. "*Everyone's* looking at you now."

I looked at them. All of them. A hundred people, glowing in rainbow light.

Seven weeks ago, it would have been my worst nightmare.

"Yeah," I said. And I laughed, wetly, helplessly, my face hot and wet and shining. "Yeah, they are."

I didn't hide.

---

## Epilogue: Toast, Again

The rainbow cherry blossoms were on the national news for three days. Scientists came from Tokyo University to study the trees. They found nothing, except that the trees were extremely healthy and, at night, glowed very faintly. The fan account hit two hundred thousand followers. Someone made a song about it. It charted.

Class 2-B won the culture festival competition by a margin of nine hundred visitors. Himemiya Reika conceded defeat with a magnificent *ohohoho*, and then, the following Saturday, she took Nijiko, Kaede, Ayumi, and me for a drive in her limousine. It did, in fact, have an aquarium. Nijiko ate one of the fish. It came out unharmed but glowing, and Himemiya decided it was now the most valuable fish in Japan, and she has since become, against all odds, a sort of friend. She comes to the rooftop at lunch sometimes. She brings fancy macarons. Nijiko says they taste like loneliness and money, which made Himemiya cry, and then laugh, and then cry again.

Kaede and Nijiko have reached what Ayumi calls "a tsundere détente." Kaede still says "It's not like I *like* you or anything" at least four times a day. Nijiko still says "I like you too, Kaede-chan!" every time. Last week I caught Kaede teaching Nijiko kendo forms on the roof after school. Nijiko had formed a sword out of her own arm. It was rainbow and very wobbly. Kaede was smiling. When she saw me, she went bright red and fell off the water tank.

Ayumi is writing a light novel about all of this. It's called *My Average Life Was Ruined by a Glittery Slime Girl*. She says it's purely fictional. It's three hundred pages long and I'm the main character and she uses my real name. I'm considering legal action.

Kurosawa-senpai and I talk now. Not about anything in particular. Poetry, mostly. He lends me books. I lend him manga. He read all of *Kiss Me Under the Starlit Greenhouse* in a week and told me, gravely, that Rintarou was "a very well-written character." I don't know if anything will come of it. I'm not in any hurry. Nijiko has been strictly forbidden from making any further announcements on my behalf, and has only violated this rule twice, both times very quietly.

And me?

I'm still Sato Mei. I'm still a hundred and fifty-eight centimeters tall. My grades are still exactly average. My hair is still brown, and I still wear my grandmother's red hair clip, although these days it's permanently tinted a gentle shade of rainbow and it sparkles a little in the sun.

I'm still embarrassed. Constantly. Every single day. When Nijiko greets me at the school gate by turning into a giant glowing banner that says GOOD MORNING MEI-CHAN. When she eats the classroom fish tank (again). When she hugs me in the hallway in front of the whole school and I come out of it glittering from head to toe. My face still goes red. My ears still burn. I still want, sometimes, to crawl under my desk and never come out.

But I don't hide anymore.

---

This morning, I was late again. I'd stayed up reading, this time because Nijiko had wanted to know how a novel ended and I'd read the last three chapters aloud to her through my bedroom window while she floated in the koi pond, glowing softly and crying rainbow tears into the water while the fish crowded around her, lit up like little lanterns.

My mother handed me toast with strawberry jam as I ran out the door, and I put it in my mouth without thinking, and I ran.

Nijiko bounced along beside me, *boing, boing, boing*, scattering sparkles in the morning light.

When we got to the corner, the one I always avoided, the blind one with the high stone wall, I stopped.

I looked at it for a long moment.

Then I took Nijiko's hand. Warm, fizzy, soft. She looked at me, and her heart crystal glowed gold, with its bright healed line running across it like a seam of sunlight.

"Ready?" I said, around the toast.

"*Ready!*"

And together, holding hands, laughing, we ran around the corner, straight into whatever was waiting on the other side.
